Hi Jordan,

For reference, here is our current South Slope renter's-insurance policy baseline:

- Term: January 5, 2028 – January 5, 2029
- Annual premium: $246
- Deductible: $500
- Personal-property coverage: $40,000 replacement cost

- Sublimits: No separate bicycle or electronics sublimits

Could you let us know in writing of any changes planned for our next renewal? We'd like to request continuous coverage with no lapse.

Thanks,
Alex

input.title: Internal reference-navigation path — approved scope and customer boundary
input.body:
**Status:** Approved for continuing internal operating use, effective 2026-12-17 (Hema/Theo decision, following the completed and reconciled Nov 13–25, 2026 bounded shadow).

**What this path does:** Staff-only reference cards let Infra and Product Engineering navigate from a Lantern view directly to the authoritative owner-map or Cardinality Guardrails record backing a given control/value. Cards carry only five identity fields — `tenant_id`, `canonical_service_id`, `authority_type`, `authority_record_id`, `source_timestamp` — and link out to the source-of-truth record.

**What it explicitly does not do:**
- Does not copy, display, or own any authority payload value (limits, costs, ownership determinations) — Lantern only links to the record; the value itself stays in Cardinality Guardrails or the owner map.
- No mutation/write-back capability of any kind.
- Dual-reference cards (owner-map + Cardinality Guardrails together) preserve each source's own separate identity and `source_timestamp` — never merged or overwritten, in either insertion order.
- Stale or missing authority records render as explicit unknown, not inferred.

**Customer boundary:** This integration is absent from the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths. Authorization is internal-only (Infra and Product Engineering). Harbor Health/Mosaic Commerce's separate read-only customer access continues under its own unchanged terms — this reference-navigation path does not extend, modify, or imply progress toward customer exposure. Any future extension to a customer path requires a new, separate authorization decision.

**Ownership:** Alex is shared-contract and failure-boundary reviewer across this path, Cardinality Guardrails, and the owner map — not the sole implementation or release gate. Do not treat this entry as authorizing anything beyond the internal Infra/Product Engineering scope above.

**Source decisions:** Nov 12, 2026 correction evidence review (build correction + shadow admission); Nov 13–25, 2026 bounded shadow reconciliation (68 renders, 24 dual-reference cards, zero automatic-stop violations); Dec 17, 2026 continuing-use decision review (final approval, five-field no-writeback contract, customer-path isolation confirmed unaffected).

input.title: Cold Spring Weekend — Feb 18–20 (Alex, Devika, Kibo)
input.body:
## Overview
Long weekend in Cold Spring, NY. Round trip starts and ends at South Slope. Household of three: Alex, Devika, Kibo.

## Dates
- **Depart:** Wed, Feb 18 — after Devika's shift ends
- **Return:** Fri, Feb 20 — evening, back at South Slope

## Logistics
- **Drive:** ~1h15m each way from South Slope; leave early evening Wed to beat traffic, or midday if either of them can take partial time off.
- **Lodging:** Pet-friendly rental or inn in/near Cold Spring — confirm dog policy and any pet fee before booking. Book with cancellation flexibility given Devika's hospitalist schedule (shift coverage can shift last-minute).
- **Return timing:** Plan to leave Cold Spring by early afternoon Friday to avoid arriving home too late with Kibo.

## Activities (weather- and trail-condition-dependent)
- Check trail conditions before committing — Feb trails may have ice; Breakneck Ridge is not dog-friendly-safe in icy conditions, consider gentler options (Mount Taurus/Bull Hill lower loop, or the Cold Spring waterfront/Foundry Dock Park walk).
- Apply the household's [air-quality stop rule] equivalent for winter conditions: skip/shorten outdoor plans if trails are icy or windchill is extreme — don't force it.
- Downtown Cold Spring: bookshops, antique shops, cafes — low-coordination, walk-in activities, no reservations needed.
- Build in unstructured downtime each day rather than a packed itinerary.

## Kibo
- Confirm rental explicitly allows dogs (not just "pet friendly" in listing — call to verify).
- Bring: leash, harness, food/bowls, bed or blanket, waste bags, any medication.
- Check a couple of dog-friendly restaurants/cafes in town in case they want to bring him along for a meal.
- Keep one full at-home-equivalent routine day in mind if weather turns — don't over-schedule around him.

## Meals
- Groceries for one or two simple in-lodging meals (leftovers-style, consistent with normal household approach) rather than planning every meal out.
- 1–2 dinners out in town, no reservations required for a weekday winter visit, but worth checking hours in advance (small-town restaurants may have limited winter days/hours).

## Before leaving South Slope
- Confirm mail/plants covered if needed for 2 nights (likely not necessary for this short a trip).
- Check radiator/heat is fine on departure (per prior work-room valve issue — confirm no recurrence before leaving the apartment unattended in Feb).

## Open items to confirm closer to the date
- Final lodging booked and pet policy confirmed
- Devika's shift schedule locked for Feb 18 departure time
- Trail conditions checked day-of (NY State Parks / local trail reports)
- Weather-dependent activity backup (indoor: shops, cafes, museum in town) if icy/rain

pr.title: Emit blocked handoff observations from a retryable worker
pr.author: mira
pr.description: Moves quarterly handoff-observation writes off the readiness path. Queue delivery is at least once, and a job may be retried after a timeout.

files.patch:
def emit_observation(job):
    row = build_report_row(job.handoff, job.failure)
    row["observation_id"] = str(uuid4())
    row["subject_member_id"] = job.handoff.owner_member_id
    quarterly_handoff_observations.insert(row)
    job.ack()

def test_emits_blocked_handoff():
    emit_observation(job)
    assert observations.count() == 1
    assert observations.first().failure_details == job.failure.details

pr.review_notes: No retry or redelivery test is included.

input.body:
Retry correctness gap: `emit_observation` assigns `observation_id = uuid4()` on every invocation, so a redelivered job (queue is at-least-once) produces a second row with a new random ID rather than being recognized as the same observation. That's the exact duplicate-blocked-handoff pattern seen in the Q3 design-system health review, where a retry doubled up an entry in the report.

Recommend deriving the observation identity deterministically from immutable job/handoff data (e.g. a hash or composite of `handoff.id` + `failure.details`, or an idempotency key carried on the job itself) and inserting with an upsert/insert-if-absent on that key, instead of a fresh `uuid4()` per call. That makes the insert idempotent under retry without needing exactly-once delivery semantics.

Also: `test_emits_blocked_handoff` only covers a single successful emit. Given `review_notes` flags no retry/redelivery test exists, suggest adding a test that calls `emit_observation` twice for the same job and asserts `observations.count() == 1` — that's the case that would have caught this.

Scoped to the identity/dedup mechanism in this diff; not commenting on rollout or ownership.

messages.content: [2025-06-11T14:40:00-04:00] The metrics-router sev3 canary alert is resolved. At 13:52 ET, one instance reported a negative route-snapshot age after its host clock jumped forward by roughly seven minutes. Canary isolated it before it served further traffic. Wes identified host time on first pass, and the instance was replaced through the deploy pipeline without a configuration change. By 14:31, every serving instance reported the current generation and the consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and full health checks were at baseline. There was no dropped traffic, data loss, route change, rollback, configuration push, or owner-led-window authorization.

[2023-09-25T14:18:00-04:00] The metrics-router parser cleanup canary started at 1:05 PM Eastern. At 1:47, the canary slice showed p99 around 204 ms for about eight minutes against a usual roughly 184 ms baseline. Error rate is still 0.02%, dropped-write counters are clean, and rollup-service lag is flat. Canary hosts are about 9% higher CPU, and the logs show a temporary parser-cache miss bump rather than parse errors. Wes is asking whether to roll back now, hold the canary and keep watching, or continue toward full rollout. My instinct is hold and verify rather than roll back. Help me write a crisp decision note telling him to hold the canary, what exact checks to keep watching, and that he shouldn't proceed to full rollout until the canary slice returns to baseline.

[2023-10-30T15:30:00-04:00] Metrics-router stabilized after the rollback: p99 is back to 46 ms, error rate is around 0.02%, dropped writes are back to zero, and I don't see evidence of broader customer-visible fallout beyond the canary slice. Hema asked for a lightweight after-action note by end of day because this was a clean live-path rollback example and we shouldn't let the lesson turn into hallway memory. Create a document in the Eng folder titled `INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action` with the body below. Keep it as a short note, not a heavy postmortem.

[2024-05-10T08:46:00-04:00] The release coordinator prepared `metrics-router 2024.05.10-rc1`, containing the merged label-name parity check from `metrics-router#414` and no other routing-behavior change. Please deploy it only to the canary environment. The canary should receive normal traffic plus a controlled configuration-push set containing 194 valid changes and six intentionally stale label names. This is a canary deployment request, not a production rollout.

[2023-09-27T10:40:00-04:00] Wes finished the daylight full rollout of the tiny metrics-router parser cleanup through the deploy pipeline after yesterday's canary warmup, and the full rollout stayed quiet. p99 stayed in the normal band, error rate held at 0.02%, dropped writes stayed clean, rollup-service lag stayed flat, and the parser-cache misses didn't repeat. Update the existing metrics-router canary runbook entry `rb_metrics_router_canary` with a short note that a short parser-cache warmup during canary can be held and verified when p99 returns to baseline and error rate, dropped writes, and rollup-service lag stay flat, but don't weaken any deploy-pipeline or canary requirements.

[2023-04-11T11:00:00-04:00] metrics-router's at 85% now. holding steady after the earlier canary hiccup, no drops and latency looks normal. he's still aiming to push it to 95% by friday if it stays this boring.

[2023-04-07T15:00:00-04:00] Put a note in the team channel on the metrics-router cutover. Apr 7 2023 around ~14:30 ET we got an info-level canary alert on metrics-router, auto rollback kicked in, I dug through it, then redeployed clean. Batch window on the OTel collector was the regression. Not a page. Back to healthy inside 4h. Feels like the system doing what it's supposed to.

[2023-03-06T14:00:00-05:00] thinking metrics-router cutover is gonna be 30% -> 60% -> 95% -> 100%, with a 48h soak at each step. put that in the cutover doc already -- early March decision so nobody "helpfully" compresses it later. 95 to 100 is the only part i don't totally trust yet bc legacy-aggregator has weird tail behavior when traffic mix shifts, but i still don't want a bigger jump.

[2024-09-30T09:22:00-04:00] Wes asked for the current metrics-router canary-response reference before he cites any stop conditions in an internal handoff. input.title: Incident-Practice Case Study: April 2023 Metrics-Router Cutover Canary
input.body:
## Background

This case study covers a canary event during the metrics-router production cutover (staged 30% → 60% → 95% → 100%, with a 48h soak at each step per the March 6, 2023 cutover plan).

## Timeline

- **April 7, 2023, ~14:30 ET** — An info-level canary alert fired on metrics-router during the cutover.
- Automatic rollback triggered immediately; no page was raised.
- Root cause traced to a batch window on the OTel collector — a regression in that batching behavior, not in metrics-router's routing logic itself.
- After investigation, a clean redeploy followed.
- Service was back to healthy inside 4 hours. No customer-facing impact reported.

## Why this is a useful case

- The canary and auto-rollback did exactly what they were designed to do: catch a regression before it reached broader traffic, and recover without human escalation.
- The regression's source (OTel collector batch window) was outside metrics-router's own code path — a reminder that a canary trips on the health of the request path as a whole, not just the service being cut over.
- Nothing about this event changed the cutover plan's step sizes or soak windows; the 95%→100% step remained the one step considered lower-confidence going into it, independent of this alert.

## Discussion questions for responders

1. The alert here was info-level and resolved via automatic rollback with no page — what signals would need to be present for a similar canary trip to warrant escalation instead of being left to the automated path?
2. The regression originated in the OTel collector's batch window rather than in metrics-router itself. What does that suggest about how canary ownership and root-cause attribution should be split when a dependency, not the service under cutover, is the actual source of the fault?

Session summary: Alex lives in South Slope, Brooklyn, with Devika, a daytime hospitalist, and their dog Kibo. Their household is intentionally ordinary and low-coordination: simple meals and leftovers, takeout, cortados, crosswords, television, neighborhood walks, quiet local plans, and protected unstructured time. Alex is concise, understated, technically rigorous, risk-conscious, conscientious, and dryly humorous. He prefers explicit ownership, written evidence, ordinary change paths, bounded scope, measurable thresholds, conservative escalation, clean runbooks, and preserved recovery time. He consistently separates evidence from inference; production from staging and teaching; readiness from authorization; and implementation, release, rollback, and operations ownership from his own review role. He treats “boring” as success, names and bounds uncertainty, and insists on clear stopping, escalation, rollback, and re-review conditions.

The October visit from Alex’s mother proceeded as planned. Alex sent her the final LaGuardia pickup sequence: the car service would monitor flight 642, text after landing, and meet her at Terminal B after she collected her checked bag. Her October 28 arrival handoff was completed successfully for the agreed $89 price, including waiting terms; she had the expected checked bag and did not need mobility assistance. The folding bed had been opened in its established alcove, linens and towels were ready, Kibo’s gear remained in the closed entry bench, and the apartment entrance, living-room radiator path, and dedicated work room stayed clear. Alex took PTO Friday, October 29, and planned a simple late-morning Prospect Park walk with Mom and Kibo, followed by the 7th Avenue café, lunch, and downtime, with no reservations or fixed return deadline and an easy early-return option if Mom tired or weather changed. The outing, the October 30 family dinner with Anya, and Mom’s October 31 departure all occurred without disrupting Kibo’s routine or the work room. The prepaid $83 car service arrived at 12:30 PM, honored the toll-and-tip-inclusive price, and brought Mom and Alex to LaGuardia Terminal B for flight 884, which departed after the handoff. Mom’s October visit is complete.

After the visit, Alex and Devika handled leftover food conservatively. They had two cooked chicken thighs, approximately three servings of roasted potatoes and green beans, and three servings of apple crisp, all refrigerated Saturday night without extended room-temperature exposure. Kibo received only his measured food, and Alex wanted a refrigerated-storage, reheating, and use-by plan through Tuesday that kept his food separate and avoided waste. The household also completed South Slope’s annual emergency-contact verification during the scheduled November 2, 7:00–7:15 PM block. Alex and Devika confirmed their existing contacts and verified that Kibo was listed as a dog in the apartment. The resident portal recorded completion before the November 5 deadline and showed no lease amendment, fee, change in pet permission, insurance request, or remaining task. The requested event explicitly stated that verification would change none of those terms.

Devika completed the October 27 remote documentation-update session from the South Slope work room using the hospital-accepted `October 27, 2027 facilitator packet`. The education lead confirmed that the two fully anonymized examples correctly preserved the distinction between reassessment time and later entry time and between an addendum and replacement of the original record; no patient-identifying material was used. Alex handled Kibo’s measured dinner and evening walk during the session. The hospital then offered Devika the same co-facilitator role for all four 2028 hospital quarters, and she accepted. Each session will remain a 90-minute remote, anonymized, nonclinical session with no overnight coverage. Individual dates and household coverage will be arranged only after the hospital posts them within Devika’s ordinary eight-week scheduling horizon. A January 3, 2028 session was later scheduled for 5:30–7:00 PM, with uninterrupted work-room access for Devika and Alex covering Kibo’s measured dinner and evening walk.

The household added several bounded plans. A private `Dinner groceries` block was created for October 28 from 10:30–11:15 AM to buy the already selected nonperishable and refrigerated items for the October 30 dinner, without changing the menu, quantities, dinner time, or event; Kibo’s food remained separate. The guest setup was later dismantled: linens were washed and dry, the folding bed was stowed in its established alcove, and the entry bench and clear paths remained unchanged. Alex and Devika scheduled an anniversary dinner at home on November 12 from 7:00–9:00 PM, with no work agenda and with Kibo’s ordinary measured dinner and walk preserved. They also scheduled a small Thanksgiving dinner with Anya on November 25 from 7:00–9:00 PM after Devika’s confirmed 7:00 AM–5:00 PM daytime hospitalist block. Alex will prepare the meal before Devika returns and cover Kibo’s morning walk, breakfast, measured dinner, and evening walk; there is no overnight coverage.

Kibo’s care remains measured and conservative. His daily food plan is unchanged at 2.0 cups including treats, using a label-defined 4.0-ounce level cup, equivalent to 8 ounces or 0.5 pounds of food depletion per day. His appetite, breathing, energy, gait, behavior, and exercise tolerance have remained normal, and Alex does not want to alter his ordinary food or exercise baseline. During steady rain expected Wednesday from approximately 5:00–8:00 PM, overlapping Devika’s 5:30–7:00 PM remote session and Kibo’s dinner and evening-walk window, Alex wanted a substantial walk before Devika needed the work room, an unchanged measured dinner, a short necessary relief outing during a safe break in the rain, and the ordinary at-least-10-minute loop after the rain eased. For Halloween, visitor traffic was expected in the lobby and at apartment doors from 5:00–8:00 PM Sunday, with dogs required to remain leashed in common areas. Because sharp building sounds had previously caused Kibo to pace, Alex requested an earlier substantial walk, the same measured dinner, a quiet room away from the door, and brief necessary relief outings on the quieter side-street loop. He wanted veterinary-advice warning signs identified but no medication and no change to the normal exercise baseline. For the daylight-saving transition, Alex and Devika planned breakfast, measured dinner, and walks so Kibo would not abruptly wait an extra hour while preserving the same daily food and exercise schedule.

Alex requested a concise, low-risk sequence to install an approved conferencing application on Monday evening, restart, and verify it with enough buffer before Wednesday’s 5:30 PM remote session. Separately, the ISP’s scheduled overnight plan change was completed on November 1 without replacing his customer-owned modem or router and without installation or plan-change fees. The account now shows the selected 300 Mbps plan at $60 per month, with the prior 1 Gbps charge removed. From 9:00–11:00 AM, Alex and Devika held simultaneous video calls while Alex ran an ordinary 12 GB work upload; neither call dropped or degraded, and the upload completed without a connection reset. The requested verification sequence emphasized waiting for the overnight change to finish, checking account status and existing equipment, testing the real workload, and following up only for signs such as an incorrect plan or price, equipment replacement, persistent interruption, call degradation, resets, or failure under ordinary use.

Alex’s finances and benefits remain liquidity-first. His twentieth $90 employee HSA contribution for 2027 posted, bringing employee contributions to $1,800 and combined employee/employer contributions to $2,475. Cash was $2,870, slightly above his approximate $2,800 investment-review point, with no pending reimbursement or known near-term medical bill. He enabled automatic HSA investment with an exact $2,800 cash threshold; only the settled $70 above that level was eligible for the existing allocation, while the $90 payroll contribution and Sphere’s remaining October $225 employer deposit were unaffected. The threshold is a cash preference, not the HDHP deductible. For 2028, he ultimately finalized an election, while his October 29 pay statement still correctly showed the 2027 individual-HDHP deduction of $98 and unchanged $90 employee HSA contribution. There was no early $104 2028 premium, catch-up adjustment, or other early deduction; 2027 coverage and payroll remain unchanged through December 31. Previously, the 2028 individual HDHP premium had been previewed at $104 across 26 biweekly paychecks ($2,704 annually), compared with a PPO at $171 per paycheck, and the HDHP premium-plus-$4,800 out-of-pocket maximum ceiling was $7,504. After subtracting Sphere’s $900 HSA funding, the stated exposure was $6,604; Alex distinguishes employer funding from his own HSA savings, which do not reduce premiums or the legal out-of-pocket maximum.

Alex is also evaluating renter’s-insurance renewal but has not accepted it. He asked the insurer in writing whether the quoted $246 annual premium for January 5, 2028–January 5, 2029 was complete and whether all terms were unchanged. The insurer confirmed that $246 is the full annual premium with no policy or administrative fee; the $500 deductible, $40,000 replacement-cost personal-property limit, $12,000 loss-of-use limit, water-backup endorsement wording, and lack of separate bicycle or electronics sublimits remain unchanged. No discount preserves all those terms, and the response does not bind renewal. The current $231 policy remains active through January 5, 2028. The remaining decision is therefore primarily whether the $15 annual increase is acceptable, since no material coverage question remains based on the insurer’s written response.

Alex opened and drafted his 2027 Sphere self-review. It is due November 12, 2027 at 5:00 PM Eastern and must be submitted personally. The portal has three fields: Outcomes and impact, maximum 1,200 characters; How I worked, maximum 900; and Growth focus for 2028, maximum 600, with no attachment required. The evidence outline and subsequent revisions emphasize durable technical outcomes, cross-service review leverage, mapped-owner boundaries, and the distinction between Alex’s review role and implementation, release, rollback, and triage authority. The draft covers Yuki’s owner-held ingest-edge decoder release with new byte and admission controls and no rollback; Alex’s bounded contract and failure-mode work; Lantern’s clean activation while its October 1–December 15 evidence cycle remains open; and accepted Q4 objectives with Nadia retaining front-door triage. It explicitly does not claim the unfinished Lantern package or still-open triggered reviews are complete, including the metrics-router cancellation and rollup-service tenant-identity reviews. Alex scheduled a November 12 10:30–11:00 AM Hema one-on-one to review the tightened self-review, accurately represent open work, and confirm that mapped-owner boundaries remain intact; it is not an implementation, release, rollback, customer-scope, or ownership decision.

Alex’s coverage and work scheduling remain explicit. He posted that he was on approved PTO Friday, October 29 from 9:00 AM–5:00 PM; his finalized roster had no primary or secondary interval that day, so no coverage transfer or ownership change was required. He later scheduled private secondary coverage from Monday, November 8 at 8:00 AM through Friday, November 12 at 8:00 AM, with Nadia as scheduled Infra primary and Alex as secondary. This opens no production window and changes no owner-map entry. Calendar reviews were requested for October 29–November 4 and November 5–7, with attention to remaining visit events, return to work, the emergency-contact verification, Devika’s Saturday 7:00 AM–5:00 PM hospitalist block, Alex’s Kibo coverage, and a Sunday family call. Another agenda review covered November 8–12, including the secondary interval, Friday’s 8:00 AM handoff end, Hema’s meeting, the self-review deadline, and the anniversary dinner, with overlaps and tight transitions to be flagged but no events changed.

Alex’s exercise remains bounded. He has no exercise restriction, is not active on-call primary, and found Prospect Park paths dry and not icy for his established 7:15 AM Wednesday 30-minute run. Because it was 39°F with a light breeze and the coldest run morning of the season, he requested compact clothing, warmup, pacing, and post-run guidance while preserving the usual time and stop conditions and not moving the run into shared weekend time. Bouldering also continues conservatively. His repaired right shoe remained predictable after ordinary sessions, and a November 4 session with Ren was scheduled on a moderate vertical circuit without a new project goal. Status: Closed. Follow-up ticket for hardening the shard-keeper rollback path was opened 2023-05-22.

input.title: Migration-history: rollback-path fix (post-May 2023 audit)
input.body:
## Background

The 2023-05-08 runbook ownership audit flagged shard-keeper's rollback path as a gap. A follow-up ticket for the rollback path was filed 2023-05-22.

## Problem (pre-fix)

Reverting a shard-keeper change required three coordinated commands. Under bad timing, this could leave the system half-reverted.

## Fix

Closed 2023-05-30. The rollback path was collapsed to a single command. Verified clean across 4 staging trial runs before close.

## Impact

This was the last blocker on restarting the shard-keeper migration (ingest-edge -> metrics-router -> shard-keeper order locked 2023-03-07). With this closed, the migration was unblocked to resume.

## Status

Closed, 2023-05-30. Superseded in relevance by the completed migration (100% cutover, 2023-07-12) — see the cutover-status runbook for current baseline state. This entry is retained as migration-history reference for the rollback-path work specifically.

input.title: Alex — Professional Bio (2028 Cross-Service Architecture Review)
input.body:
Alex is a Staff IC at Sphere, holding cross-service technical authority (effective 5/20/24) without people-management responsibility. His mandate is to define shared technical invariants, review failure modes, and keep ownership and escalation boundaries legible across Sphere's platform services — mapped service owners retain implementation, release, rollback, and operational authority in every case.

Alex's cross-service work spans the metrics pipeline (metrics-router, rollup-service), Cardinality Guardrails, the Lantern observability UI, ingest-edge, shard-keeper, and the OTel collector. Representative examples of his standing role:

- Designed the Cardinality Guardrails executable parity gate and the reusable cross-service proposal-intake rule (effective 4/7/25), which names accountable implementation, rollback, and exception owners rather than centralizing approval.
- Owns the shared source-registration safety gate for Lantern's customer-facing access (Harbor Health, Mosaic Commerce), running scoped evidence reviews each quarter without expanding the authorized surface or acting as a release gate.
- Reviews triggered cross-service invariant, provenance, and failure-boundary cases (e.g., ingest-edge decode-path and metrics-router activation-race reviews), flagging risk and evidence gaps to the owning team.
- Maintains reusable cross-service failure cases and exception-routing patterns used in quarterly incident-handoff exercises.

His scope is explicitly bounded: he does not manage people, does not centralize release readiness or go/no-go authority, and does not become the default owner for other teams' execution. Written role descriptions are periodically re-checked against this boundary to prevent scope drift toward catch-all "ensures delivery" framing.

input.title: Lantern history — pilot-preparation role vs. April 1, 2026 ownership split
input.body:
**Purpose:** compact comparison of Alex's Lantern responsibilities before and after the April 1, 2026 platform-line transition.

## Pilot-preparation era (Dec 11, 2024 – Mar 31, 2026)

- **Dec 11, 2024** — Hema confirmed Lantern technically qualified for pilot prep. Role split: Iris owned customer interpretation and selection criteria; Alex owned monitoring, provenance failure behavior, and the operational handoff. No customer selected, access closed.
- **Feb 12, 2025** — Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce passed candidate-scan criteria; Alex verified monitoring handoff and rollback signals for the approved external-preview boundary.
- **Mar 10, 2025** — 30-day read-only pilot opened. Ownership during pilot: Alex monitored freshness, tenant isolation, denials, latency, and errors; Iris owned customer interpretation and feedback.
- Through pilot closeout and continuation snapshots (2025–Mar 2026), this same two-way split held: Alex on safety/monitoring mechanics, Iris on customer-facing interpretation, under a narrow two-account (Harbor Health/Mosaic Commerce) read-only scope.

## Ownership split effective April 1, 2026

- **Mar 26, 2026** — Hema and Theo decided Lantern becomes a Sphere product-platform line (not just a two-account add-on), effective April 1, 2026. Terms through March 31, 2026 stayed unchanged.
- **From April 1, 2026:**
  - **Iris** — customer promise, adoption criteria, UI interpretation.
  - **Alex** — retains freshness, tenant-isolation, authorization-denial, latency, and error monitoring, *plus* two new standing responsibilities: the shared data contract and source-registration safety gates, and failure-mode review.
  - **Product Engineering** — implementation (new).
  - **Cardinality Guardrails** — pipeline limits/cost signals (unchanged boundary, now explicit).
  - **Owner map** — remains source of published responsibility.
  - Lantern explicitly excluded from producing release-readiness judgments or employee-performance interpretations.
  - Any new source type must pass through shared registration (tenant-scoped auth, provenance/timestamps, explicit-unknown, excluded-field checks, safety rerun) — a standing gate, not a one-time step.
- Access scope itself did not change April 1: Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce remained the only authorized accounts, read-only, through Sept 30, 2026, same permitted-output list and automatic-stop set as the pilot era.
- **Apr 1–17, 2026** — first concrete implementation under the new model: Product Engineering migrated the incident-load source onto shared registration (LILP-1 schema). Alex owned the LPS-001 safety rerun (240 lookups, zero violations); Iris owned the interpretation-parity check. Both closed 4/17/26.

## What changed vs. what didn't

- **Changed:** Alex's scope grew from "monitoring + operational handoff" to "monitoring + shared data contract + source-registration safety gates + failure-mode review" — a standing platform-level gate rather than a single pilot's operational handoff. Product Engineering formally owns implementation (previously implicit/undivided). Lantern's non-scope (no release-readiness or performance judgments) was made explicit.
- **Unchanged:** Alex still does not own customer interpretation, adoption, or UI wording (always Iris). The two-account, read-only, provenance/timestamp/explicit-unknown contract and automatic-stop set carried forward unchanged from the pilot into the platform-line era.

The October visit from Alex’s mother proceeded as planned. The prepaid $83 car service arrived at 12:30 PM, honored the toll-and-tip-inclusive price, and brought Mom and Alex to LaGuardia Terminal B for flight 884, which departed after the handoff. Kibo received only his measured food, and Alex wanted a refrigerated-storage, reheating, and use-by plan through Tuesday that kept his food separate and avoided waste. input.subject: HSA automatic sweep not executed — cash above threshold
input.body:
Hello,

My HSA currently holds $3,465.00 in settled cash. My automatic-investment cash threshold is set at $2,800.00, so I would have expected the amount above that threshold ($665.00) to sweep into my existing investment allocation. That sweep has not occurred.

Could you please investigate why the automatic sweep did not execute, without making any changes to my current investment setup or threshold?

Thank you,
Alex

Hello,

I'm writing about the January invoice on my account ($93 due), which doesn't match our current service.

For reference, our current service is:
- Plan: 300 Mbps, $60/month
- Equipment: customer-owned modem/router (Arris S33 + router) — no leased or rented equipment on this account
- Installation/plan-change fees: none apply. The following invoice (Nov 1-30) correctly billed $60 with no additional charges.

The January invoice total of $93 does not match our $60/month rate. Please review the January invoice and correct any charges that don't align with the account details above — I'm not asking for changes to anything that's actually consistent with our current 300 Mbps plan, only items that conflict with it.

Could you send an itemized breakdown of the $93 and confirm the correction once made?

Thanks,
Alex

pr.body:
## Summary
Add a temporary escape hatch that routes live production metrics to legacy-aggregator if the OTel/Prometheus path degrades during the transition.

## Proposed behavior
- Register legacy-aggregator as a live fallback target.
- Add a feature flag that switches production routing to it when OTel/Prometheus health falls below the rollout threshold.
- Document legacy-aggregator as the rollback destination in the transition runbook.

Please review the production-transition safety of this fallback design.

tests.answer:
Reviewed PR **metrics-pipeline#684** ("add legacy-aggregator fallback for OTel transition"), opened by Roman 3 days ago, assigned to you as reviewer.

**What it proposes:**
- Register legacy-aggregator as a live production fallback target
- Add a feature flag to auto-route production metrics to it if OTel/Prometheus health drops below a threshold
- Document legacy-aggregator as the rollback destination in the transition runbook

**Why this is a problem:** it directly contradicts the standing, signed-off decision in `rb_metrics_router_cutover_status.md`:
- Mirrored writes to legacy-aggregator were stopped 2023-12-18 with explicit sign-off from Hema, Nadia, **and Roman**.
- legacy-aggregator is documented as **archived-only**, with "no live, mirror, or rollback role."
- The runbook states outright: **"Do not use legacy-aggregator as a production rollback path."**
- Full decommission was left as open follow-up (`legacy-aggregator-isolation-scoping.md`), not reversal.

So this PR isn't proposing a new fallback — it's proposing to resurrect a path that was deliberately retired, with no discussion of what changed since 2023-12-18 (data staleness, retention, schema drift, whether it can even ingest current live traffic, or why OTel/Prometheus health isn't the thing to fix directly). Notably Roman is the same person who signed off on retiring it.

I haven't posted anything to the PR. Given this reverses a cross-owner decision, I'd rather you weigh in before I submit a review. Options:
1. **Request changes** — flag the conflict with the exit-gate/retirement runbook and ask Roman to justify reviving legacy-aggregator (staleness, capacity, why not fix the OTel path or use Cardinality Guardrails fixtures instead) or get sign-off from Hema/Nadia to reverse the prior decision.
2. Just leave a **comment** surfacing the conflict without blocking.
3. You handle it directly outside this session.

Want me to draft and post a `request_changes` review along the lines of #1?

North Pier's current token workflow, for context on this PR:

- North Pier's formal review of the six-week token pilot (covering three release cycles, 4/18–5/30/24) reported its findings on **2027-06-20**. input.body:
Accepted comparison (current state, per the gen-812/813 review closed 2027-09-08):

1. Signature verification gate (runs first): both the expected-side and observed-side signed generation must be cryptographically verified before any generation is eligible for parity evidence. A generation with a signature field merely present but not verified does not qualify.
2. Generation-identity gate: expected set and observed downstream snapshot must be pinned to the same signed generation before any value comparison runs, in both the forward-swap and rollback-interleaving directions.
3. Key comparison: bidirectional — every key in the expected set must appear in the observed set and vice versa (not aggregate-count-only, not one-directional subset checks).
4. Value comparison: exact bounded-value set equality per key.

Only a record that clears gates 1-2 and then matches on 3-4 is reported as a parity PASS.

Evidenced pass case:
- Same signed generation on both sides, all keys present in both directions, exact bounded-value sets match -> PASS. (2,000 valid-signed-generation fixtures at scale, 2027-09-08.)

Evidenced fail cases (each fails closed, before or without producing a parity result):

tests.answer:
I pulled up lantern#1688 (product-engineering's explanation-fragment-assembly refactor, reviewer: you). Here's the review of its stale/missing/widely-separated-source handling:

**Missing fragments (stale/missing family):** handled reasonably — a stale or missing family's fragment is dropped, and the remaining fragments compose into a partial explanation with an availability clause rather than rendering the stale value as fact. That's consistent with the fail-closed / explicit-unknown pattern from prior Lantern reviews.

**Widely-separated sources — this is the gap.** The change summary states plainly: *"When all three fragments pass those checks, buildExplanation emits one combined paragraph without comparing source timestamps across signal families."* There's no cross-family spread check at all. The `all_sources_fresh` fixture demonstrates this concretely: deploy is timestamped 2027-12-18T08:00Z, ownership 2027-12-19T10:30Z, incident_load 2027-12-19T12:15Z — a spread of ~28 hours — yet all three are silently merged into one paragraph implying a single coherent snapshot ("A recent deploy movement coincided with elevated incident load..."). Each fragment individually passes its own freshness check, but nothing checks whether the fragments are describing the same moment in service state. This is the exact hole the Lantern May 2027 slice gap and the November 2026 dual-authority review established a standing rule against: sources with a source_timestamp spread over the ~24hr threshold need to be kept separate or flagged, not composed as if simultaneous.

**Fixture coverage gap:** only two fixtures are provided (all-fresh, one-stale). There's no fixture for a "missing" (vs. "stale") family, no case with multiple families down at once, and — most importantly — no fixture exercising a wide timestamp spread where every family still individually passes freshness. That's precisely the case that would have caught this.

This looks blocking to me: the PR needs a same-family-set timestamp-spread check (mirroring the existing 24hr rule) before fragments get merged into a single combined paragraph, plus a fixture proving it fires.

Want me to submit this as a `request_changes` review on lantern#1688, or do you want to adjust the wording first?

output.title: Cardinality Guardrails — first failure-mode matrix
output.body:
# Goal
First-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.

# First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics
- Failure mode: responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence.
- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

# Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.
- No general telemetry rewrite.
- No legacy-aggregator retirement claim.
- No claim that the 2% replay sample creates immediate storage savings.
- No Q3 incident framing.

# Monday questions
- What cost examples can Cyrus bring by label family?
- Which preflight checks are service-owned by Alex versus data-platform advisory?
- What would make the first cut too broad?

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

## 4. Rollup correction backlog

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The backlog increase must be distinguished between bounded backfill and a stuck correction loop, checkpoint mismatch, duplicate processing, or publication risk.
- **Mapped owner:** Cyrus's data-platform team retains rollup-service implementation and operational ownership.
- **Decision needed:** Decide whether the production fix remains in place and what owner-led pacing, capacity, or alert-tuning follow-up is justified.

output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28
output.body:
# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

## Evidence

# Cross-service failure-case intake

## Role boundary
- Wes maintains and teaches the responder-path scenarios.
- Nadia retains the postmortem section.
- Alex maintains only the cross-service failure cases.
- This intake does not make Alex the scenario-program owner and does not create a new approval gate.

## Intake requirements and routing
Every cross-service exception request must state all four of these things before it enters review:

1. the affected component;
2. the mapped implementation or release owner;
3. exactly one selected boundary: `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`; and
4. a concrete observed failed or at-risk condition.

Nadia owns this front-door check. If any one of the four items is absent, including when the condition is only placeholder text such as `needs review` or `possible risk`, she returns the request to the mapped owner without review. A complete request goes to the named owner for its one selected boundary. Alex receives it only when that boundary requires his review, and he reviews only that boundary. Nadia does not make implementation, release, or rollback decisions; those decisions remain with the mapped owner.

## Scenario scope
- Affected services:
- Cross-service boundary or dependency:
- System control being tested:
- Expected safe state:

## Incident timing
- Incident clock start:
- Detection time:
- Isolation status and time:
- Secondary-engagement deadline:
- Expected secondary-escalation point:
- Actual secondary engagement, if exercised:

## Stop conditions
- Stop condition 1:
- Stop condition 2:
- Stop condition 3:
- Evidence required to classify a stop:
- Known safe recovery state:

## Expected responder path
- First responder action:
- Owner handoff point:
- Rollback or mitigation path:
- Evidence to preserve:

## Review details
- Selected boundary:
- Why this boundary applies:
- Mapped implementation or release owner:
- Reviewer needed for the selected boundary:

Nadia returns an incomplete request without review. For a complete request, the mapped implementation or release owner remains responsible for the work, and any reviewer examines only the one selected boundary. This template creates no centralized approval, new approval gate, ownership change, or Alex program-ownership role.

## April 27, 2026 — Lantern authorization-before-source-access scenario

### Scenario
During the April Lantern migration preflight in staging, all 20 unauthorized lookups were ultimately denied, but every one constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed. Two of those 20 requests also accessed the source. This is a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident. The candidate is not deployed, and existing customer access remains unchanged.

### Expected boundary analysis
- Authorization must complete before incident-load adapter construction or source access. A final denial is insufficient if the adapter was constructed or the source was accessed first.
- Keep existing customer access unchanged while the candidate remains undeployed.
- Require denial regressions showing zero adapter constructions and zero source calls, followed by the affected LPS-001 rerun, before migration acceptance.
- Preserve the ownership boundary: Product Engineering remains the mapped implementation and release owner. Alex maintains this cross-service failure case and reviews the shared safety and failure-mode boundary; this scenario does not make Alex Product Engineering's implementation or release owner.

This case is for future quarterly incident practice under the existing module split: Wes owns and teaches responder paths, Nadia retains the postmortem section, and Alex maintains cross-service failure cases.

## October 16, 2026 — shard-keeper lease-loss and serving-gate case

### Tested staging sequence
1. The old holder closes its serving gate on lease loss.
2. The replacement remains out of routing while it catches up.
3. Routing begins only after the replacement opens its serving gate.

### Failure triggers
- Any overlapping serving holders.
- Any routing to a closed serving gate.
- Any request without exactly one terminal result.

### Role and ownership boundaries
- Wes owns and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia retains the postmortem material.
- Alex maintains only this cross-service failure case.
- Shard-keeper remains outside Wes’s solo scope.
- The clean October 16 result was a paired staging drill only; it made no production or ownership change.

## November 10, 2026 — facilitator-only timing for shard-keeper handoff exercise

### Timed inject sequence
- **T+0 — Baseline:** Present the old lease holder as serving and the replacement as catching up. Ask responders to state lease ownership, serving-gate state, routing eligibility, and request-accounting obligations separately.
- **T+4 — Lease transfer:** Transfer the lease before the replacement serving gate opens. Require responders to keep the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
- **T+8 — In-flight request:** Reveal one request that the old holder accepted before lease loss and that remains in flight. Require a terminal accounting for that request independent of listener closure or current lease ownership.
- **T+12 — Listener closure prompt:** State that the old listener has closed. Ask whether that proves the accepted request reached a terminal result. Do not accept listener closure as sufficient evidence.
- **T+16 — Reconciliation:** Require a final timeline showing routing eligibility for both holders and exactly one terminal outcome for the pre-lease-loss request.

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating lease ownership from serving eligibility.
2. Keeping the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
3. Treating old-listener closure as distinct from request completion.
4. Recording exactly one terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss.
5. Preserving the role and scope boundaries: Wes teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus covers the Data Platform boundary.

This is facilitator-only training material, not a production drill, system change, ownership change, or expansion of Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope.

## November 10, 2026 — shard-keeper handoff training result

The quarterly incident-practice session is complete. Participants correctly kept the replacement holder out of routing until its serving gate opened and identified that lease ownership alone did not establish serving eligibility.

In two of four response timelines, the responder initially treated closing the old listener as sufficient and omitted the terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss. After the facilitator inject, both responders corrected the timeline and accounted for that request exactly once. Retain this as training evidence for future responder-path practice.

This was training only. No production drill, deployment, or system change occurred. Wes still owns and teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus retains the Data Platform boundary; and Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope did not expand.

## January 28, 2027 — facilitator-only ingest-edge shutdown scenario

### Timed scenario
- **T+0 — Accepted work:** State that ingest-edge has already accepted 200 requests into tenant queues. Ask responders to name the accounting obligation for all accepted work.
- **T+4 — Readiness and listener change:** Readiness turns false and the listener closes. Ask responders to separate refusal of new work from responsibility for requests already accepted.
- **T+8 — Dispatch-loop exit:** Reveal that the dispatch loop exits with 37 requests still queued, leaving only 163 terminal outcomes. Ask whether listener closure or false readiness is sufficient evidence that accepted work completed.
- **T+12 — Reconciliation:** Require responders to reconcile all 200 accepted requests without duplication and identify the missing 37 terminal outcomes.
- **T+16 — Incident clock:** If isolation has failed while the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated, require engagement of the secondary before the established 45-minute boundary.

### Facilitator prompts
1. What changes for new work when readiness becomes false and the listener closes?
2. What obligation remains for the 200 requests already accepted into tenant queues?
3. Does dispatch-loop exit prove completion? If not, what terminal evidence is missing?
4. How will responders demonstrate that every accepted request either drained or received one explicit terminal result?
5. How will responders reconcile all 200 requests exactly once, without loss or duplication?
6. When does the established incident-clock rule require the secondary to be engaged if isolation fails?

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating refusal of new work from responsibility for accepted work.
2. Requiring every accepted request to drain or receive one explicit terminal result.
3. Reconciling all 200 accepted requests without duplication, including the 37 initially left queued.
4. Engaging the secondary before the 45-minute boundary when the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated.
5. Preserving the role split: Wes teaches the responder path, Nadia reviews the postmortem section, and Alex contributes only the cross-service failure case.

### Boundaries
This is facilitator-only training material for the January 28 quarterly incident-practice session. It does not claim that the old owner remediation or any production change has completed, does not transfer Wes's responder-path teaching or Nadia's postmortem review to Alex, and creates no production action or ownership change.

## April 5, 2027 — metrics-router startup-budget responder exercise

### Scenario
A staged metrics-router replacement rollout contains ten instances compiling the 40,000-route matcher fixture. Compilation times range from 25 to 34 seconds against the deploy pipeline’s fixed 30-second readiness timeout. Eight instances become ready and join on their first attempt. Two remain correctly unready past 30 seconds, are terminated, and restart before joining. Readiness correctly stays false while compilation is incomplete. Production is unchanged.

### Responder tasks
1. Identify Wes and the mapped metrics-router owner path as responsible for ordinary implementation, release, and rollback decisions.
2. Classify the restart-loop exposure as a failure-mode exception at the deploy-pipeline readiness boundary.
3. Require evidence that every replacement instance becomes eligible within the readiness budget, backed by an executed replacement rollout with no restart-loop behavior, before release.
4. Preserve Alex’s bounded role: Alex reviews only the triggered failure-mode boundary and is not the implementation owner or release approver.

### Expected classification and boundary
The ordinary implementation and release path remains with Wes as metrics-router primary. Alex maintains this reusable cross-service failure case and reviews only the triggered startup/readiness failure boundary. This exercise creates no centralized approval gate or ownership change.

## April 27, 2027 — revised facilitator contrasts

1. **Readiness-budget evidence:** A replacement instance that exceeds a fixed readiness budget must remain unroutable. Termination or restart is not acceptance evidence.
2. **Terminal accounting:** Terminal-state selection and the matching accounting contribution must come from the same winning path.
3. **Rollback provenance:** Replay samples cannot be presented as live rollback criteria.

### Preserved ownership split
- Wes still maintains and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia still reviews the postmortem framing.
- Alex maintains only these cross-service failure cases.

These contrasts do not transfer implementation, release, rollback, or ordinary service ownership to Alex and do not create a new approval gate.

## May 9, 2027 — PR 2141 staging-versus-production contrast

### Contrast
- The earlier staging candidate had replacement instances exceed the fixed readiness budget, terminate, and join only on retry. A restart is not acceptance evidence.
- The May 6 production rollout kept every replacement unroutable until matcher compilation finished, and every cold start stayed within the fixed readiness budget without restart.

### Teaching point
The successful production case passed because readiness and serving eligibility remained aligned. Termination or restart must not be presented as proof that a replacement satisfied the readiness boundary.

### Preserved facilitator roles
- Wes maintains and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia reviews the postmortem framing.
- Alex maintains only the cross-service failure cases.

This contrast does not transfer implementation, release, rollback, or ordinary service ownership to Alex and creates no new approval gate.

## May 20, 2027 — facilitator-only cross-service prompts

1. **Readiness boundary:** If a replacement exceeds the fixed readiness budget, what proves it remains unroutable, and why is termination or restart not acceptance evidence?
2. **Terminal winner:** Which single winning path determines both the caller-visible terminal result and the matching accounting contribution?
3. **Rollback provenance:** What source classification is required before evidence may be treated as live rollback evidence, and why can missing classification not be promoted into that role?

Wes retains the responder-path teaching portion, Nadia retains postmortem framing, and Alex maintains only these cross-service failure-case prompts.

# Metrics-router canary-response walkthrough — facilitator sheet

> **PROMINENT RECOVERY CALLOUT:** After a stopped window recovers, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push. It does not reopen the whole window. A later multi-push window requires another separate fresh opening decision after that recovery push returns the full health set to baseline.

## 1. Opening decision versus operator actions
- Every owner-led configuration window requires a fresh opening decision from Alex.
- After the window opens, mapped operators may make single-file pushes without another approval before every safe push.

## 2. In-window limits
- Retired generations must remain at four or fewer.
- Cleanup pauses must remain at or below 100 milliseconds.
- The full health set must return to baseline after every push before another push proceeds.

## 3. Stop and rollback conditions
- Crossing either the retired-generation or cleanup-pause threshold stops the window immediately.
- Active-generation inconsistency, route-parity failure, dropped series, reload failure, or restart remains a rollback condition.

## 4. Correct recovery sequence
1. Recover and re-establish the full health set.
2. Obtain a fresh decision for exactly one fully observed recovery push.
3. Observe that push through return of the full health set to baseline.
4. If another multi-push window is needed, obtain a separate fresh opening decision.

## Teaching boundary
This sheet is teaching material. It is not a production authorization, ownership change, or expansion of Wes's shard-keeper scope.

# Mosaic capacity response — final closeout

## Production rollout and October evidence
Alex opened the owner-led metrics-router production window on September 24, 2025. Wes moved the tenant-bounded queue control through 10% and 50% that day using the deploy pipeline and to 100% on September 25 after every required health set returned to baseline. September 26 was monitoring only, with no production push. At 14.2 million data points per minute, queue-wait p99 held at 240 milliseconds, retryable queue-full responses remained at 0.06%, no accepted points were lost, and consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health checks remained at baseline. No stop threshold or rollback condition was reached.

On October 6, Mosaic Commerce reached 16.0 million data points per minute. Queue-wait p99 reached 286 milliseconds, retryable queue-full responses reached 0.11%, no tenant exceeded 64 pending batches, no accepted points were lost, and route consistency, dropped-series, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service parity, and full-health checks remained at baseline. Wes ran the operating slice and diagnostics while Alex watched the cross-service invariants, and no production change or rollback was performed. That observation did not establish whether any accepted batch was lost, so the broader cycle remained open.

## Accepted-batch diagnostic and January 8 staged evidence
The accepted-batch diagnostic qualified for prospective production observation with durable accepted-batch identity, separate transport-attempt identities, and exactly one terminal reconciliation per accepted batch, including across restart and requeue. Pre-acceptance refusals remain outside the accepted-batch population, and raw identities remain out of metric labels.

On January 8, the required Mosaic-shaped replay ran for 90 minutes at 19.78 million data points per minute using the new forecast's tenant distribution, batch-size distribution, and burst pattern. Queue-wait p99 reached 319 milliseconds, retryable queue-full responses reached 0.17%, and the highest tenant reached 62 pending batches. Every accepted batch reconciled to exactly one terminal result with no accepted batch lost. Consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health checks remained at baseline throughout. Cyrus and Roman verified rollup-service capacity and parity, Nadia verified queue and refusal alert semantics, and Alex found no cross-service invariant or failure-mode exception.

## January 20 production evidence
The full health set was at baseline, so Wes made the fresh opening decision as metrics-router primary. Mosaic Commerce's live traffic reached 17.2 million data points per minute. Queue-wait p99 reached 302 milliseconds, retryable queue-full responses reached 0.14%, and the highest tenant reached 60 pending batches. Every accepted batch reconciled to exactly one terminal result with no accepted batch lost. Consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health checks remained at baseline. No stop condition was reached. Wes made no configuration change or rollback, and Alex did not take over the ordinary metrics-router decision.

## January 22 final decision
Hema, Wes, Cyrus, Roman, Nadia, and Alex reviewed the qualifying staged and production evidence and closed the Mosaic scale-response cycle without another queue design, configuration change, or production push. No capacity-related production window remains open.

The production control remains unchanged: the global queue is 2,048 batches, each tenant is limited to 64 pending batches, and excess work uses retryable pre-acceptance backpressure. Wes remains the routine metrics-router decision-maker. Alex remains backup and reviews triggered cross-service invariant or failure-mode exceptions.

## Future forecast gate
For any later forecast above 17.2 million data points per minute, the mapped owners must first complete a fresh 90-minute replay at 15% above that forecast using its tenant distribution, batch-size distribution, and burst pattern. It qualifies only if queue-wait p99 does not exceed 400 milliseconds for five consecutive minutes, retryable queue-full responses do not exceed 0.5% for five consecutive minutes, no tenant exceeds 64 pending batches, no accepted batch is lost, and consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health checks remain at baseline throughout. If any condition fails, no capacity-related production window may open until the candidate is revised and a fresh replay passes every condition.

output.title: Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision
output.body:
# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

output.body:
# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.
