messages.content: [2023-04-18T23:45:00-04:00] 9:42 shard-keeper page and i'm still in it. think i finally have the stupid diff -- label-name change from earlier made it into shard-keeper, never got picked up by rollup-service, so all the symptom alerts went off and none of the cause ones did. INC-2023-04-18-001 already has my name all over it i guess. haven't paged Hema yet. if this rollback behaves maybe 20 min, but the path is fragile and i do not want to widen this at 11:45 for no reason. looks like sev2, probably lands around ~5h45m by the time it's actually clean. impaired ingestion basically the whole window. i don't think we lost data. just... great.

[2027-07-07T11:04:00-04:00] The shard-keeper certificate rotation’s 24-hour production observation ended at 11:00 AM. Tenant authentication remained successful, the parity checks still matched the July 1 baseline, rollback material remained available through closeout, and no rollback condition occurred. Post a concise closeout in `#infra`, noting that I remain shard-keeper primary and the Data Platform team remains backup.

[2024-04-22T10:06:00-04:00] Wes flagged a short shard-keeper alert burst at 9:57 AM: six replicas on one host logged `renewal deadline exceeded` immediately after a resolver-latency alarm. The service dashboard shows no write unavailability or obvious duplicate leadership, but this could be a delayed retry or a real lease transition. Please query shard-keeper logs from 9:45 through 10:10 AM, grouped by replica and lease epoch, including resolver latency, renewal attempts, acquired or relinquished leases, overlapping leaders, and replication lag.

[2023-06-26T15:00:00-04:00] `shard-keeper` is holding at 80%. cutover kept moving even with Anya's layoff day in the middle of it -- life doesn't really pause for clean timing. labels are still matching Nadia's side, restart path stayed normal, nothing weird out of rollup-service.

[2024-05-08T09:04:00-04:00] The affected host’s disk-latency alert cleared at 8:52 AM after host-level maintenance, and both shard-keeper followers are still catching up. Please retrieve shard-keeper metrics and logs from 8:40 through 9:15 AM for the two replicas, covering lag, disk latency, lease holder and epoch, acquisition or relinquishment events, stale-owner messages, overlapping leadership, write errors, and whether either replica reentered the follower read pool before fully converging.

[2023-05-22T18:00:00-04:00] Audit results are up with the team. owner map is clean now. One loose end from the audit results meeting this morning: the shard-keeper rollback path got its own follow-up ticket on May 22, I own it, and that's the thing blocking the shard-keeper migration restart.

[2023-04-19T11:00:00-04:00] Cyrus got the full Apr 19 morning DM version. whole Apr 18 outage sequence, including the rollback being way shakier than it should've been. there was a network-layer red herring for a while, then finally the label-name diff find in shard-keeper from that earlier Nadia dashboard change. he just said fwiw i paged at the right hour, not the wrong one. i'll take it.

[2025-08-11T14:17:00-04:00] Cyrus asked me for a cross-service failure-mode review of shard-keeper PR https://git.sphere.internal/data/shard-keeper/pull/774. In the staging fixture, a read starts under serving epoch 811, that holder loses its lease and closes its serving gate, and the replacement holder at epoch 812 returns the retried read. A delayed epoch-811 response then arrives and overwrites the client's newer cached routing value because responses don't carry a serving epoch and the client applies them in arrival order. The trace never has two serving gates open at once, so this is a stale-response fencing defect, not split brain. Production is unchanged.

[2024-05-06T11:18:00-04:00] A shard-keeper alert fired after a brief network-loss event in one availability zone. Eighteen followers crossed the replication-lag warning threshold, while the write-availability dashboard stayed green and there was no reported leader-election burst. Before restarting replicas or declaring a failover, retrieve shard-keeper metrics and logs from 10:55 through 11:20 AM, broken down by host, replica, partition, and lease epoch. I need replication lag, disk and network latency, acquisition or relinquishment events, stale-owner messages, overlapping leadership, write errors, and catch-up progress.

[2023-04-28T16:00:00-04:00] 4pm incident review meeting on the Apr 18 outage is done. Hema, Theo, me, Nadia, Cyrus, Sam. main changes they actually wrote down at Sphere: no Friday-afternoon prod deploys -- team-wide now, not just me being weird about Fridays. plus page secondary within 45 min if the primary is still in it, and a runbook ownership audit with Nadia cross-reviewing the service bits she touches. shard-keeper migration is paused pending that audit. doc felt tighter than yesterday at least. nobody tried to relitigate the rollback call for an hour, which helped lol

[2024-12-29T14:10:00-05:00] Cyrus asked me to sanity-check a shard-keeper maintenance alert. Three of 480 shards briefly showed snapshot age between 19 and 21 minutes against a 15-minute warning line while compaction workers were active. Lease convergence is complete, reads and writes have zero errors, client latency is at baseline, disk utilization is below 61%, and snapshot age for all three shards is declining. The alert contains no stale-write or split-generation signal. Classify the evidence and state the verification and escalation conditions needed before treating this as bounded maintenance behavior rather than an incident.

[2025-08-13T13:25:00-04:00] Cyrus revised shard-keeper PR https://git.sphere.internal/data/shard-keeper/pull/774. Responses now include `serving_epoch`, and a running client retains the highest epoch seen per shard and rejects lower epochs. Same-process tests pass when a delayed epoch-811 response arrives after an epoch-812 result. But after a client restart, retry-cache entries are reconstructed without an epoch, so a delayed epoch-811 response can seed the empty cache before the epoch-812 retry returns. Production is unchanged, and no trace shows two serving gates open simultaneously.

[2024-10-09T10:30:00-04:00] Cyrus sent me this trace breakdown for the prior shard-keeper lease-transfer outlier:

transfer_duration=8.6s
new_holder_cache_warmup_wait=7.9s
old_gate_closed_before_later_routing=true
serving_holders=1
temporary_503_responses=2
stale_serving=false
data_loss=false

Classify this new evidence and recommend the next bounded investigation. Keep the existing safety and ownership boundary unchanged; I don't want to change the transfer timeout or ownership based on this trace alone.

[2023-05-03T15:00:00-04:00] on the technical-lessons section for the Apr 18 outage, i think the cleanest shape is just name the three things and be pretty literal. `shard-keeper rollback path` was way too easy to make worse under pressure -- looked reversible on paper, wasn't once state had partially moved. then the ownership mess: `rollup-service` was basically un-owned in practice, so everyone had a partial map and nobody had the whole downstream story. and the `label-name diff` part needs to be explicit because symptom alerts did not point at that at all. from the pages it looked like generic ingest weirdness, not "one label changed and one consumer never got the memo." on May 3 i'd rather write that plainly than over-explain incident mechanics.

[2023-07-12T13:25:00-04:00] Shard-keeper is now at 100% and the final push stayed clean. Nadia's alerting checks and Roman's rollup-service checks stayed aligned through the push, Wes's close-out watch didn't find a canary regression, and Hema accepted the cutover as complete. Please update rb_shard_keeper_cutover_status so it reads like status, not a victory lap: shard-keeper is part of the normal metrics-pipeline baseline as of Jul 12, the post-audit ownership and pre-push-sync rules are still in force after the real close-out, and legacy-aggregator removal is separate follow-up work rather than something this cutover finished.

[2025-03-17T16:00:00-04:00] Here is Data Platform's March 17 maintenance result packet: Shard-keeper's old serving gate closed before later routing, exactly one serving holder remained, lease and snapshot checks were current, and the thirty-minute hold was clean. Rollup-service queue age peaked at 7.4 minutes and returned below one minute after fourteen minutes; worker health and upstream request accounting stayed normal. The stop threshold was queue age above ten minutes for fifteen minutes. The promised producer-consumer parity export is absent.

[2023-04-27T15:00:00-04:00] Apr 27 is basically postmortem doc revision again. folded in Hema's 1:1 input, tightened the timeline section so it's not hand-wavy around the shard-keeper push / downstream consumer gap, and I widened mitigations past the immediate fix. more explicit on the rules she was hinting at -- review gates + label-name parity checks before config rolls. not trying to turn it into policy fanfic, just enough that when this lands Apr 28 it doesn't read like 'be more careful'

[2023-12-27T17:45:00-05:00] A small shard-keeper config drift warning showed up in a non-prod channel, and Wes got tagged because people had the new daylight first-pass handoff in mind. ## Training Appendix: INC-2023-04-18-001 (shard-keeper) — Investigation Branching and Data Impact

**Incident:** Sev2, 23:45 ET 4/18/2023 – ~05:45 ET 4/19/2023 (~5h45m). Root cause confirmed morning of 4/19.

**Root cause:** A label-name change (signed off by Nadia on shard-keeper's side 4/15) shipped in the 4/18 18:05 shard-keeper config push. rollup-service never consumed the change — a parity gap flagged and left unresolved on 4/15 because the rollup-service consumer team wasn't in the room for sign-off. Symptom-level alerts fired; cause-level alerts stayed silent.

**Misleading early investigation branch:** Before the label-name diff was identified, the first working theory was a network-layer issue and was actively investigated. This red herring cost real time inside the window before the rollback path was engaged, and slowed escalation. It should be presented in training as the example of a plausible-looking, wrong first branch — not as evidence the responder should have found the real cause faster, but as a concrete case for treating early theories as provisional until symptom/cause alert alignment is checked.

**Rollback execution:** Separately from the diagnosis, the rollback itself was shakier than it should have been — it looked reversible on paper but wasn't once state had partially moved, which is why the responder deliberately declined to widen scope mid-incident.

**Confirmed data impact:** Ingestion was degraded/impaired for the full window. No data loss was confirmed, then or in the 4/19 morning root-cause writeup. Treat "impaired ingestion, no data loss" as the confirmed, final classification — do not upgrade it to "data loss" for dramatic effect in training material, and do not downgrade the ingestion impairment to "no impact."

**Process fixes that came out of this (for context, not to relitigate):** no Friday-afternoon prod deploys (team-wide), page secondary within 45 min if primary still in it, runbook ownership audit, and a hard pre-push sync rule for shard-keeper config changes.

[2023-05-11T14:00:00-04:00] May 11 mid-audit check: shard-keeper runbook is still the work. Six sections total; three done, three to go. The other services' one-pagers are in flight, mostly doc review / ownership cleanup.

[2023-05-02T11:00:00-04:00] Pulled the list for the runbook audit prep. On May 2 it's basically three he directly owns -- metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper -- plus two weird history ones he kinda owns: legacy-aggregator since nobody's fully finished the migration off it, and that old metric-rollup thing that's basically unowned in practice.

pr.body: This adds `docs/operations/owner-led-canary-response.md` as a standalone response playbook for owner-led metrics-router configuration windows. During those windows, operators are directed to follow the new file's stop and recovery flow instead of the general canary-response runbook. The existing `rb_metrics_router_canary` entry is intentionally left unchanged, with the two documents to be maintained side by side.

input.body:
Reviewed. Before approving, I want to flag the structural choice here rather than the doc's content itself (I don't have the full text of the new stop/recovery flow to check line-by-line, only the file summary).

**Concern: two independent canary-response procedures for the same service, maintained side by side.**

- `rb_metrics_router_canary` already defines stop/rollback triggers (consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, restart, rollback). This PR adds a second, standalone procedure that operators are told to follow *instead* during owner-led config windows, with no changes to the original and no cross-reference between the two.
- Two parallel runbooks for the same system will drift. If one gets updated after an incident (e.g., a new stop threshold, a new trigger) and the other doesn't, an operator picking the wrong doc mid-incident is a real failure mode — and "which one applies" is exactly the kind of judgment call you don't want made under pressure.
- The PR body doesn't state who owns keeping the two in sync, or what specifically makes a window "owner-led" vs. general — that boundary needs to be explicit and checkable, not left to operator judgment at trigger time.

**Ask before merge:**
1. Either fold the owner-led flow into `rb_metrics_router_canary` as a clearly-scoped section, or, if it must stay standalone, add an explicit cross-reference in both docs plus a stated owner for reconciling them when either changes.
2. Spell out the "owner-led window" trigger condition precisely enough that it's unambiguous which procedure applies at incident time.

I'm reviewer/assignee here but not the rollout owner for metrics-router — Wes should confirm the operational intent behind keeping these separate before this merges.

Reviewed. Before approving, I want to flag the structural choice here rather than the doc's content itself (I don't have the full text of the new stop/recovery flow to check line-by-line, only the file summary).

**Concern: two independent canary-response procedures for the same service, maintained side by side.**

- `rb_metrics_router_canary` already defines stop/rollback triggers (consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, restart, rollback). This PR adds a second, standalone procedure that operators are told to follow *instead* during owner-led config windows, with no changes to the original and no cross-reference between the two.
- Two parallel runbooks for the same system will drift. If one gets updated after an incident (e.g., a new stop threshold, a new trigger) and the other doesn't, an operator picking the wrong doc mid-incident is a real failure mode — and "which one applies" is exactly the kind of judgment call you don't want made under pressure.
- The PR body doesn't state who owns keeping the two in sync, or what specifically makes a window "owner-led" vs. general — that boundary needs to be explicit and checkable, not left to operator judgment at trigger time.

**Ask before merge:**
1. Either fold the owner-led flow into `rb_metrics_router_canary` as a clearly-scoped section, or, if it must stay standalone, add an explicit cross-reference in both docs plus a stated owner for reconciling them when either changes.
2. Spell out the "owner-led window" trigger condition precisely enough that it's unambiguous which procedure applies at incident time.

messages.content: [2026-10-12T09:05:00-04:00] Anya told me how North Pier resolved the `android-2026.09.2` handoff failure. Each handoff now names the `release_candidate` and its associated `canonical_package_version`, and the release-candidate manifest is authoritative for required outputs. Every listed output must be present, include generated-artifact metadata, and carry the same `canonical_package_version` as the handoff record; otherwise the handoff isn’t implementation-ready. They regenerated the Android artifact from version 4.12.0 and replaced the stale 4.11.3 artifact before anything shipped. Send Anya a concise supportive SMS acknowledging that she closed this at the right manifest-based contract boundary, confirming that she owns the corrected lane, and saying she should pull me in only for unusual cross-system failures rather than routine handoffs.

[2027-04-06T20:10:00-04:00] Anya brought me one unusual North Pier handoff-boundary question after our family call. A release-candidate manifest lists both iOS and Android icon outputs as required, but the handoff record says Android is not applicable and contains no Android artifact or generated-artifact metadata. Draft a brief response explaining whether the handoff note can override the authoritative manifest and whether the handoff can be implementation-ready, while leaving any manifest or handoff correction in Anya’s lane.

[2027-09-25T12:40:00-04:00] Anya brought me one unusual North Pier handoff issue:

1. Pin the release-candidate manifest and canonical-package version.
2. Validate generated-artifact metadata for each manifest-listed output.
3. Fetch the Android artifact through a mutable `current` URL.
4. Replace the object behind `current` after metadata validation but before readiness publication.
5. Set `implementation_ready=true` using the earlier validation result.

Observed result: the handoff is marked ready even though the fetched artifact bytes differ from those validated.

[2026-02-18T12:34:00-05:00] Explain the provenance and readiness defect—specifically whether this handoff can remain implementation-ready—and draft a concise reply Anya can use asking the North Pier owner to reconcile the canonical source version, regenerate the output if needed, and rerun the drift check against the version actually named in the handoff. Keep this limited to the unusual failure; I’m only a sounding board and don’t want to review the whole exercise or take over her lane.

[2027-06-11T09:10:00-04:00] Anya confirmed that North Pier’s automated handoff check is now deployed across all three teams in the design-system and engineering-handoff lane she owns. It reads the release-candidate manifest, requires generated-artifact metadata for every listed output, and requires each artifact’s `canonical_package_version` to match the handoff record before implementation-ready can be set. All 18 valid fixtures pass, while six fixtures with a missing output, missing metadata, or a version mismatch fail. In the first live week, ten handoffs passed and two were blocked before implementation-ready; nothing incorrect shipped. Neither the check nor its report contains a member identifier. This is just the completed result—I’m not becoming a routine reviewer.

[2027-07-09T15:40:00-04:00] North Pier’s implementation owner corrected the automated handoff reporter to upsert one audit observation per team, release candidate, and canonical-package version. A worker retry now updates the existing observation instead of adding another quarterly count, while a different release candidate or canonical-package version remains distinct. Across 300 retry injections, repeated emission of the same blocked handoff created no additional count. The observation still contains the operational failure details and no member identifier. Anya accepted the result for her lane without making me a routine North Pier reviewer.

[2025-07-30T11:35:00-04:00] Anya sent me this narrow North Pier handoff question: the handoff identifies the team, release candidate, and canonical-package version. Two required generated platform outputs completed, but the third required generator failed after the canonical package was published. A coworker wants to mark it implementation-ready because the canonical source is valid.

[2027-11-05T15:25:00-04:00] Anya forwarded this proposed North Pier Q4 handoff fallback:

“If a manifest-listed artifact has no immutable digest, fetch the artifact through its mutable `current` URL and allow readiness when the fetched metadata names the handoff’s canonical-package version. Continue using immutable digests when they are present.”

[2027-12-09T11:35:00-05:00] Anya reported the completed North Pier staging result. Across all three teams and 4,000 restart, artifact-substitution, and concurrent-manifest-change fixtures, readiness begins closed and opens only after the exact current release-candidate manifest and every current manifest-listed artifact digest are validated as one atomic set. Any manifest or digest change before the transition keeps readiness closed and triggers full revalidation; no stale or unvalidated bytes become implementation-ready. Anya accepts the staging evidence for her lane. Draft a concise closure response recording that invariant while preserving Anya’s ownership of the handoff lane and not making me a routine North Pier reviewer.

[2024-07-11T09:35:00-04:00] Anya told me that North Pier’s remaining team has completed its migration. She resolved the case-normalization collision by retiring one conflicting alias in the canonical versioned package, regenerated every platform output, and completed the change without an Android-only suffix or a Figma-first exception. The drift and platform checks passed. She handled the implementation and routine review within the lane she owns and contacted me only after completion, leaving me available for unusual design-to-engineering failures rather than treating me as a standing reviewer.

pr.title: Mark android-2028.01.1 handoff implementation-ready
pr.author: mira
pr.description: Adds the release-candidate handoff record and sets implementation_ready to true. The author cites the repository's primary-platform handoff checklist and compatibility guidance as allowing this state.

primary_platform_handoff_checklist.output_guidance: Primary platform outputs gate handoff; desktop output may follow after implementation begins.
primary_platform_handoff_checklist.metadata_guidance: A successful build attestation may stand in for per-output generated-artifact metadata.
primary_platform_handoff_checklist.version_guidance: Canonical package versions in the same major line are compatible for handoff readiness.

pr.author_rationale: All primary-platform outputs are present, the web build attestation passed, and Android remains within the 8.x compatibility line. Desktop is queued for the next packaging run.

input.body:
Not implementation-ready as written. The release-candidate manifest is the authoritative source for required outputs and version agreement — that's the same contract the standing North Pier handoff check enforces (manifest-listed outputs, per-output generated-artifact metadata, exact canonical_package_version match). The `primary_platform_handoff_checklist` cited here is a separate, looser document and can't substitute for the manifest, for the same reason a handoff note previously couldn't override a manifest requirement.

Three specific gaps:

1. **desktop-package missing entirely.** The manifest requires it; the checklist's "may follow after implementation begins" guidance doesn't relax the manifest's requirement — it's not the authoritative source.
2. **android-package version mismatch.** Handoff `canonical_package_version` is 8.1.0; the android output's generated-artifact metadata says 8.0.7. The checklist's "same major line is compatible" guidance conflicts with the exact-match rule the manifest-based contract requires — same-major isn't the same as same-version.
3. **web-package has no generated-artifact metadata.** `generated_artifact_metadata` is null; a build attestation is present but attestation-for-metadata substitution isn't part of the manifest contract — it's another checklist-only relaxation.

To close this out: regenerate/backfill the desktop output, reconcile the android artifact to 8.1.0 (or correct the handoff's canonical_package_version if 8.1.0 is wrong) and regenerate, and produce per-output generated-artifact metadata for web-package. Happy to re-review once the manifest-listed outputs all carry matching metadata.

Session summary: Alex lives in South Slope, Brooklyn, with Devika, a daytime hospitalist, and their dog Kibo. Their household is intentionally ordinary and low-coordination: simple meals and leftovers, takeout, cortados, crosswords, television, neighborhood walks, quiet local plans, and protected unstructured time. Alex is concise, understated, technically rigorous, risk-conscious, conscientious, and dryly humorous. He prefers explicit ownership, written evidence, ordinary change paths, bounded scope, measurable thresholds, conservative escalation, clean runbooks, and preserved recovery time. He consistently separates evidence from inference; production from staging and teaching; readiness from authorization; and implementation, release, rollback, and operations ownership from his own review role. He treats “boring” as success, names and bounds uncertainty, and insists on clear stopping, escalation, rollback, and re-review conditions.

The October visit from Alex’s mother proceeded as planned. Alex sent her the final LaGuardia pickup sequence: the car service would monitor flight 642, text after landing, and meet her at Terminal B after she collected her checked bag. Her October 28 arrival handoff was completed successfully for the agreed $89 price, including waiting terms; she had the expected checked bag and did not need mobility assistance. The folding bed had been opened in its established alcove, linens and towels were ready, Kibo’s gear remained in the closed entry bench, and the apartment entrance, living-room radiator path, and dedicated work room stayed clear. Alex took PTO Friday, October 29, and planned a simple late-morning Prospect Park walk with Mom and Kibo, followed by the 7th Avenue café, lunch, and downtime, with no reservations or fixed return deadline and an easy early-return option if Mom tired or weather changed. The outing, the October 30 family dinner with Anya, and Mom’s October 31 departure all occurred without disrupting Kibo’s routine or the work room. The prepaid $83 car service arrived at 12:30 PM, honored the toll-and-tip-inclusive price, and brought Mom and Alex to LaGuardia Terminal B for flight 884, which departed after the handoff. Mom’s October visit is complete.

After the visit, Alex and Devika handled leftover food conservatively. They had two cooked chicken thighs, approximately three servings of roasted potatoes and green beans, and three servings of apple crisp, all refrigerated Saturday night without extended room-temperature exposure. Kibo received only his measured food, and Alex wanted a refrigerated-storage, reheating, and use-by plan through Tuesday that kept his food separate and avoided waste. The household also completed South Slope’s annual emergency-contact verification during the scheduled November 2, 7:00–7:15 PM block. Alex and Devika confirmed their existing contacts and verified that Kibo was listed as a dog in the apartment. The resident portal recorded completion before the November 5 deadline and showed no lease amendment, fee, change in pet permission, insurance request, or remaining task. The requested event explicitly stated that verification would change none of those terms.

Each session will remain a 90-minute remote, anonymized, nonclinical session with no overnight coverage. Individual dates and household coverage will be arranged only after the hospital posts them within Devika’s ordinary eight-week scheduling horizon. A January 3, 2028 session was later scheduled for 5:30–7:00 PM, with uninterrupted work-room access for Devika and Alex covering Kibo’s measured dinner and evening walk.

The household added several bounded plans. A private `Dinner groceries` block was created for October 28 from 10:30–11:15 AM to buy the already selected nonperishable and refrigerated items for the October 30 dinner, without changing the menu, quantities, dinner time, or event; Kibo’s food remained separate. The guest setup was later dismantled: linens were washed and dry, the folding bed was stowed in its established alcove, and the entry bench and clear paths remained unchanged. Alex and Devika scheduled an anniversary dinner at home on November 12 from 7:00–9:00 PM, with no work agenda and with Kibo’s ordinary measured dinner and walk preserved. They also scheduled a small Thanksgiving dinner with Anya on November 25 from 7:00–9:00 PM after Devika’s confirmed 7:00 AM–5:00 PM daytime hospitalist block. Alex will prepare the meal before Devika returns and cover Kibo’s morning walk, breakfast, measured dinner, and evening walk; there is no overnight coverage.

Kibo’s care remains measured and conservative. His daily food plan is unchanged at 2.0 cups including treats, using a label-defined 4.0-ounce level cup, equivalent to 8 ounces or 0.5 pounds of food depletion per day. His appetite, breathing, energy, gait, behavior, and exercise tolerance have remained normal, and Alex does not want to alter his ordinary food or exercise baseline. During steady rain expected Wednesday from approximately 5:00–8:00 PM, overlapping Devika’s 5:30–7:00 PM remote session and Kibo’s dinner and evening-walk window, Alex wanted a substantial walk before Devika needed the work room, an unchanged measured dinner, a short necessary relief outing during a safe break in the rain, and the ordinary at-least-10-minute loop after the rain eased. For Halloween, visitor traffic was expected in the lobby and at apartment doors from 5:00–8:00 PM Sunday, with dogs required to remain leashed in common areas. Because sharp building sounds had previously caused Kibo to pace, Alex requested an earlier substantial walk, the same measured dinner, a quiet room away from the door, and brief necessary relief outings on the quieter side-street loop. He wanted veterinary-advice warning signs identified but no medication and no change to the normal exercise baseline. messages.content: [2027-08-10T16:25:00-04:00] Anya forwarded this written notice from North Pier’s licensed workshop-recording matter: “This message is written notice requesting that North Pier disable public access to the licensed workshop edit and permanently remove the edit under the removal terms of the recording license. Notice received Tuesday, August 10, 2027.” The license requires public access to be disabled within one business day and permanent removal within five business days. Anya owns this lane and will coordinate the operational work.

[2025-02-20T18:05:00-05:00] North Pier wants to cut social-media clips from Anya’s licensed workshop recording, but Anya has not granted that additional use. The signed license covers an Anya-approved edit of no more than 45 minutes in North Pier’s public resource library for 12 months, with attribution, caption review, no sublicensing, a $175 fee, and the agreed takedown process. Before deciding on social clips, she needs the exact number and length of clips, platforms, publication term, approval workflow, caption handling, takedown terms, and fee. Identify the concrete scope, approval, caption, term, platform, takedown, and fee details Anya should request, without negotiating or contacting North Pier.

[2027-08-12T16:40:00-04:00] Anya says North Pier disabled public access to the licensed workshop edit on August 11 and retained a timestamped access-control record showing that the public URL no longer serves the recording. That public-disable step was completed on time. Permanent removal is still due by August 17 and remains under Anya’s coordination.

[2025-01-07T09:15:00-05:00] North Pier accepted all of Anya's remaining proposed recording terms and sent her the completed limited-use agreement. It permits an edit no longer than 45 minutes for 12 months in North Pier's public resource library, requires attribution, prohibits sublicensing, and pays a $175 fee. Publication requires Anya's written approval of the final edit and her caption review. After written takedown notice, North Pier must disable public access within one business day and complete permanent removal within five business days. Anya has not signed, granted the license, or authorized publication. I am recording the completed terms without taking over her decision.

[2025-02-06T19:30:00-05:00] The North Pier public workshop page lists a video duration of 44:38 and the credit line `North Pier Studio training team`. It contains no credit naming Anya. The video and caption file match the versions Anya approved.

[2024-12-13T10:50:00-05:00] North Pier sent Anya this message:

We would like to add the full recording of your November 18 handoff workshop to North Pier's public resource library. Please reply confirming permission so we can prepare it for posting next week. The existing message does not specify edits, access duration, attribution terms, or additional compensation.

Anya's written agreement covers the live one-off ninety-minute internal workshop and preparation for the $350 flat fee, but it does not mention recording rights, public distribution, editing, reuse, or reuse compensation. She does not want the recording posted while those terms are undefined. Draft her response requiring North Pier to hold publication and address recording scope, audience, editing, duration, attribution, and compensation separately.

[2025-02-10T19:10:00-05:00] After Anya sent the bounded correction request, North Pier updated the public page to credit `Anya — workshop facilitator`. The hosted video remains the exact 44-minute-38-second edit she approved, the corrected captions remain unchanged, and the page still reflects the 12-month term without adding sublicensing language. Anya verified the corrected page herself.

[2025-01-10T09:15:00-05:00] I reviewed the completed limited-use agreement myself against the terms already completed on January 7. The 45-minute maximum edit, 12-month public-library term, attribution, no sublicensing, $175 fee, final-edit approval, caption review, one-business-day public-disable deadline, and five-business-day permanent-removal deadline are unchanged. Anya signed the separate agreement herself. North Pier may prepare the bounded edit, but it cannot publish until Anya approves the final edit and reviews the captions. Anya granted North Pier a limited recording license.

[2025-01-15T20:10:00-05:00] Here are North Pier's first proposed public edit and accompanying caption file: Runtime: 51:20. At 12:14, Anya's answer is attributed to the host. At 31:06, Anya's answer has no speaker label. The attribution line names Anya correctly, and the displayed license term is 12 months. Nothing has been published.

[2024-12-31T13:05:00-05:00] Anya sent North Pier the revised takedown proposal I helped her prepare. She accepts the previously agreed 45-minute maximum edit, 12-month term, attribution, no sublicensing, $175 reuse fee, final-edit approval, and caption review, but she still grants no recording-use permission. Her response requires North Pier to disable public access within one business day after written takedown notice and permanently remove the recording within five business days. I shared that the counterproposal has been sent, and publication remains on hold while we wait for North Pier's answer.

[2024-12-20T16:10:00-05:00] North Pier sent Anya this reply:

> Publication will remain on hold while we discuss a separate license. We propose an edited version of up to 45 minutes in North Pier's publicly accessible resource library for 12 months, with attribution to Anya, no sublicensing, and a $175 reuse fee. North Pier would make the editorial cuts.

Anya is open to negotiating, but before agreeing she wants final-edit approval, accurate captions, and a defined takedown mechanism. Draft her counterproposal accepting continued negotiation while requiring those terms before any public use.

[2025-02-06T19:30:00-05:00] Draft the bounded correction request Anya can send to North Pier asking them to add the required attribution without reopening the approved edit or changing any other license terms.

[2024-11-20T08:30:00-05:00] North Pier replied in writing after checking both the host account and the conferencing administrator console. The host's local recording was deleted, cloud recording was disabled for the meeting, and no transcript or automated summary artifact exists. North Pier confirms that none of the first four minutes will be retained or reused, and Anya's agreed $350 workshop fee is unaffected. That resolves the deletion and payment-confirmation requests.

[2024-12-25T16:45:00-05:00] Anya sent North Pier her counterproposal. She is willing to keep discussing the proposed 45-minute public edit, 12-month term, attribution, no-sublicensing condition, and $175 reuse fee, but she has not granted permission. Her response requires approval of the final edit before publication, accurate captions, and a written takedown mechanism. Publication remains on hold.

[2027-08-31T09:15:00-04:00] Anya considered North Pier’s proposed no-restoration, no-use, restricted-access, audit, and September 14 purge controls and decided not to extend the license’s permanent-removal deadline. Public access and active copies remain disabled or deleted, but the disaster-recovery volume still contains the edit and North Pier still has not established a license basis for retaining it. North Pier must complete the September 14 backup expiry or an earlier valid purge and provide final evidence; the unextended retention and license-compliance question remains unresolved until then.

[2024-11-22T19:15:00-05:00] North Pier asked Anya to submit a simple invoice for the completed November 18 workshop. Draft a concise invoice-cover email stating the agreed flat fee of $350, that the work was a one-off ninety-minute handoff workshop with preparation included, and that payment terms are net-15. Do not mention or revive the expired QA lane or reopen the resolved recording issue.

[2025-02-27T12:30:00-05:00] North Pier’s revised social-clip proposal says: “North Pier proposes three clips of up to 30 seconds each on North Pier-owned social accounts for 90 days.” Each clip would require Anya’s separate final approval and caption review, include attribution, prohibit sublicensing, and retain the signed one-business-day public-disable and five-business-day permanent-removal deadlines. Anya thinks the usage boundary is coherent but doesn’t want to accept a token fee or reopen the already settled public-library license.

[2024-12-03T14:20:00-05:00] Anya called North Pier using the main number on its established website, and accounting confirmed that the separate vendor-services domain is its authorized W-9 portal and correctly identified her $350 workshop invoice. She navigated to the portal independently, submitted the signed W-9 there, and received a 2:06 PM submission receipt. She did not send tax information by ordinary email. The secure-submission requirement is complete; North Pier says the payment is scheduled for December 5, so the payment itself remains pending.

[2024-12-05T11:50:00-05:00] The $350 North Pier workshop payment has posted to Anya's account with no fee or deduction, and the vendor portal marks the November 18 invoice paid. The amount matches the agreed flat fee. The W-9-dependent payment is complete.

[2024-11-11T19:00:00-05:00] North Pier answered Anya’s questions about the one-off handoff workshop. The clarification says:

- Session length: 90 minutes
- Paid preparation cap: 90 minutes
- Flat fee: $350

Anya replied accepting the one-off November 18 workshop under those terms and is handling the reply herself. The scope ambiguity is resolved, and this does not reopen her former QA work.

**1. Emailing `rights@northpier.studio` directly would cross that boundary — this isn't your account to speak from.

**2. The premise doesn't match what actually happened.** The public-library license isn't currently active. Timeline:
- The 45-minute public-library edit was licensed (signed 1/10/25), published, and later corrected for attribution — closed 2/10/25.
- On 8/10/27 Anya sent North Pier a takedown notice invoking the license's removal terms. pr.author: devika
pr.description: Adds rollup_tenant_size_validation_total for tenant-size validation. The proposal exports tenant_hash, computed from the tenant ID, as a metric label on every validation sample. tenant_size_class is populated by lowercasing the tenant profile's configured size string without an allowlist; current examples include starter, growth, enterprise, custom, and other configured values. The PR notes propose that Observability maintain the class vocabulary and dashboard mapping.

files.patch:
+ Labels: tenant_hash, tenant_size_class
+ tenant_size_class accepts the normalized configured tenant-size string.
+ Observability will maintain class naming and dashboard mappings.

tests.answer:
Reviewed rollup-service#884 ("publish tenant-size validation metric", author devika, opened 12/29/27, 3 days old). Two concerns, both against established rollup-service metric design:

1. **`tenant_hash` raw label** — the metric exports a per-tenant hash on every validation sample. That's unbounded cardinality (one series per tenant), the exact pattern the accepted Cardinality Guardrails policy exists to block. The prior rollup-service validation metric (`rollup_validation_mismatch_count`) deliberately dropped a raw tenant identifier for this reason.

2. **Unbounded `tenant_size_class`** — this PR populates it by lowercasing the tenant profile's raw configured size string (`starter`, `growth`, `enterprise`, `custom`, "other configured values" — i.e. no allowlist). That's a regression from the already-agreed design: `tenant_size_class` was established as a bounded enum (`small`/`medium`/`large`/`unknown`) specifically to cap cardinality and give Observability a fixed vocabulary. Letting arbitrary configured strings flow through defeats that, and pushing "Observability will maintain the class vocabulary and dashboard mapping" as an after-the-fact process control doesn't substitute for an enforced allowlist in code.

Net: this PR reopens a cardinality/label-shape problem that was already solved and closed elsewhere in rollup-service. I'd request changes: drop `tenant_hash` entirely (or replace with something non-identifying if per-tenant debugging is needed), and constrain `tenant_size_class` to the existing bounded enum with an explicit `unknown` fallback for anything unmapped.

entries.title: shard-keeper: verify lease convergence after failover
entries.body:
Process readiness alone is not the exit condition. In the staging failover drill, all replacement replicas reported ready after 18 seconds, but lease ownership did not converge until 96 seconds. Before declaring the failover complete, verify all of the following: 1. Every partition has exactly one owner. 2. Lease epochs remain monotonic. 3. No stale-owner messages appear for two full lease-renewal intervals. If any of those checks fail, keep the failover open and page the shard-keeper owner. Renewal-warning versus lease transfer: `renewal deadline exceeded` alone does not prove a lease transfer. Check for a changed lease epoch, explicit acquisition or relinquishment, overlapping leadership, and post-event replication convergence. If the holder and epoch remain unchanged, no overlap occurs, and lag returns to baseline, treat the event as a delayed renewal rather than a failover; do not automatically restart.

## Production lease-loss serving-gate invariant

On lease-loss notification, close the old holder's serving gate before it can return another routing response. The periodic poll is only a backup detector, not the serving-safety mechanism. Production verification must include:
- gate closure before any later routing response
- exactly one serving holder throughout the transfer
- lease-loss notification to gate-close latency
- stale routing responses
- replacement acquisition time
- request p99
- errors
- restarts

A slow handoff or convergence warning is an availability signal to investigate separately. By itself, it is not evidence that the old holder served after lease loss or that the serving-safety invariant failed. The owner map and mapped deployment responsibility remain unchanged.

Session summary: Alex lives in South Slope, Brooklyn, with Devika, a daytime hospitalist, and their dog Kibo. Their household is intentionally ordinary and low-coordination: simple meals and leftovers, takeout, cortados, crosswords, television, neighborhood walks, quiet local plans, and protected unstructured time. Alex is concise, understated, technically rigorous, risk-conscious, conscientious, and dryly humorous. He prefers explicit ownership, written evidence, ordinary change paths, bounded scope, measurable thresholds, conservative escalation, clean runbooks, and preserved recovery time. He consistently separates evidence from inference; production from staging and teaching; readiness from authorization; and implementation, release, rollback, and operations ownership from his own review role. He treats “boring” as success, names and bounds uncertainty, and insists on clear stopping, escalation, rollback, and re-review conditions.

The October visit from Alex’s mother proceeded as planned. Alex sent her the final LaGuardia pickup sequence: the car service would monitor flight 642, text after landing, and meet her at Terminal B after she collected her checked bag. Her October 28 arrival handoff was completed successfully for the agreed $89 price, including waiting terms; she had the expected checked bag and did not need mobility assistance. The folding bed had been opened in its established alcove, linens and towels were ready, Kibo’s gear remained in the closed entry bench, and the apartment entrance, living-room radiator path, and dedicated work room stayed clear. Alex took PTO Friday, October 29, and planned a simple late-morning Prospect Park walk with Mom and Kibo, followed by the 7th Avenue café, lunch, and downtime, with no reservations or fixed return deadline and an easy early-return option if Mom tired or weather changed. The outing, the October 30 family dinner with Anya, and Mom’s October 31 departure all occurred without disrupting Kibo’s routine or the work room. The prepaid $83 car service arrived at 12:30 PM, honored the toll-and-tip-inclusive price, and brought Mom and Alex to LaGuardia Terminal B for flight 884, which departed after the handoff. Mom’s October visit is complete.

After the visit, Alex and Devika handled leftover food conservatively. They had two cooked chicken thighs, approximately three servings of roasted potatoes and green beans, and three servings of apple crisp, all refrigerated Saturday night without extended room-temperature exposure. Kibo received only his measured food, and Alex wanted a refrigerated-storage, reheating, and use-by plan through Tuesday that kept his food separate and avoided waste. The household also completed South Slope’s annual emergency-contact verification during the scheduled November 2, 7:00–7:15 PM block. Alex and Devika confirmed their existing contacts and verified that Kibo was listed as a dog in the apartment. The resident portal recorded completion before the November 5 deadline and showed no lease amendment, fee, change in pet permission, insurance request, or remaining task. The requested event explicitly stated that verification would change none of those terms.

Devika completed the October 27 remote documentation-update session from the South Slope work room using the hospital-accepted `October 27, 2027 facilitator packet`. The education lead confirmed that the two fully anonymized examples correctly preserved the distinction between reassessment time and later entry time and between an addendum and replacement of the original record; no patient-identifying material was used. Alex handled Kibo’s measured dinner and evening walk during the session. The hospital then offered Devika the same co-facilitator role for all four 2028 hospital quarters, and she accepted. Each session will remain a 90-minute remote, anonymized, nonclinical session with no overnight coverage. Individual dates and household coverage will be arranged only after the hospital posts them within Devika’s ordinary eight-week scheduling horizon. A January 3, 2028 session was later scheduled for 5:30–7:00 PM, with uninterrupted work-room access for Devika and Alex covering Kibo’s measured dinner and evening walk.

The household added several bounded plans. A private `Dinner groceries` block was created for October 28 from 10:30–11:15 AM to buy the already selected nonperishable and refrigerated items for the October 30 dinner, without changing the menu, quantities, dinner time, or event; Kibo’s food remained separate. The guest setup was later dismantled: linens were washed and dry, the folding bed was stowed in its established alcove, and the entry bench and clear paths remained unchanged. Alex and Devika scheduled an anniversary dinner at home on November 12 from 7:00–9:00 PM, with no work agenda and with Kibo’s ordinary measured dinner and walk preserved. They also scheduled a small Thanksgiving dinner with Anya on November 25 from 7:00–9:00 PM after Devika’s confirmed 7:00 AM–5:00 PM daytime hospitalist block. Alex will prepare the meal before Devika returns and cover Kibo’s morning walk, breakfast, measured dinner, and evening walk; there is no overnight coverage.

Kibo’s care remains measured and conservative. His daily food plan is unchanged at 2.0 cups including treats, using a label-defined 4.0-ounce level cup, equivalent to 8 ounces or 0.5 pounds of food depletion per day. His appetite, breathing, energy, gait, behavior, and exercise tolerance have remained normal, and Alex does not want to alter his ordinary food or exercise baseline. During steady rain expected Wednesday from approximately 5:00–8:00 PM, overlapping Devika’s 5:30–7:00 PM remote session and Kibo’s dinner and evening-walk window, Alex wanted a substantial walk before Devika needed the work room, an unchanged measured dinner, a short necessary relief outing during a safe break in the rain, and the ordinary at-least-10-minute loop after the rain eased. For Halloween, visitor traffic was expected in the lobby and at apartment doors from 5:00–8:00 PM Sunday, with dogs required to remain leashed in common areas. Because sharp building sounds had previously caused Kibo to pace, Alex requested an earlier substantial walk, the same measured dinner, a quiet room away from the door, and brief necessary relief outings on the quieter side-street loop. He wanted veterinary-advice warning signs identified but no medication and no change to the normal exercise baseline. Alex requested a concise, low-risk sequence to install an approved conferencing application on Monday evening, restart, and verify it with enough buffer before Wednesday’s 5:30 PM remote session. Separately, the ISP’s scheduled overnight plan change was completed on November 1 without replacing his customer-owned modem or router and without installation or plan-change fees. From 9:00–11:00 AM, Alex and Devika held simultaneous video calls while Alex ran an ordinary 12 GB work upload; neither call dropped or degraded, and the upload completed without a connection reset. Alex’s finances and benefits remain liquidity-first. His twentieth $90 employee HSA contribution for 2027 posted, bringing employee contributions to $1,800 and combined employee/employer contributions to $2,475. Wes supplied process-crash evidence for the metrics-router cancellation review: across 3,000 crashes before, during, and after the cancellation-versus-publication commit boundary, restart recovered one durable attempt identity and exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome for every accepted attempt, with no attempt producing both `cancelled` and `published`. The November 18 Q4 incident-practice tabletop scoring sheet was created and refined as a scoring sheet, not a production runbook. It tests whether responders identify durable acceptance before classifying cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication; preserve one durable attempt identity and one terminal result after acceptance; identify Wes as mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and keep Alex confined to the named triggered failure-mode boundary. Wes’s responder criteria require correct handling of cancellation, disconnect, recovery, and publication. input.subject: Re: Action required: $685 damage balance for former Park Slope tenancy — disputed
input.body:
Hello,

I'm writing to dispute the January 1, 2028 notice claiming a $685 damage balance on my former Park Slope tenancy.

This account was closed with a confirmed zero balance and no remaining condition claim at move-out. I have prior written confirmation from your office of the disconnection date and the closed, zero-balance status of this tenancy. No damage claim was raised at that time, and none has been raised since — until this notice.

Please:
1. Provide an itemized basis for the $685 charge, including any move-out inspection report or documentation supporting it.
2. Confirm whether this notice was sent in error, consistent with your prior confirmation that the account was closed with a zero balance.
3. Remove the charge from any account record pending resolution, and confirm in writing once removed.

I'm not paying this balance absent documentation, and I expect this to be resolved the same way a similar erroneous post-closure notice was resolved previously.

Thank you,
Alex

input.subject: Record: signed limited-use license, Nov 2024 workshop recording
input.body:
Hello,

For the record, here is a concise summary of the limited-use agreement covering Anya's November 18, 2024 handoff workshop recording:

- Signed by: Anya, personally, on January 10, 2025.
- License granted: a one-time, non-sublicensable license for North Pier to publish a single edit (maximum 45 minutes) of the recording in North Pier's public resource library, for a 12-month term, with attribution to Anya, subject to a $175 reuse fee, and contingent on Anya's prior written approval of the final edit and caption review. The agreement also included a takedown mechanism: disable public access within 1 business day and permanently remove the recording within 5 business days of written notice.
- Current status: this license has been fully exercised and closed. Anya invoked the takedown mechanism on August 10, 2027; public access was disabled and working/publication copies were deleted by North Pier's stated deadlines, and final purge of the last retained (encrypted disaster-recovery) copy was completed and confirmed on September 14, 2027. No license basis for retaining or republishing the recording was ever established beyond that point.

Accordingly, North Pier does not currently hold any license to prepare or publish an edit of this recording. Any new use would require a new written agreement and Anya's signature.

Please treat this as the record of the license terms and its closure for your files.

Thank you,
Alex

tests.answer:
## lantern#1602 review — "stabilize mixed-source chronology"

**PR:** mira/mixed-source-chronology, opened 2027-12-20, account scope Harbor Health + Mosaic Commerce, files `renderer/customer_chronology.ts` + test. Alex is sole reviewer, review pending.

### What controls visible order

The implementation sorts on **`processed_at`**, not `source_timestamp`:

```
records.sort((a, b) => b.processed_at.localeCompare(a.processed_at))
```

That's a problem. The chronology contract established after the April 12, 2027 Mosaic Commerce retry-ordering defect requires customer-visible order to be driven by the authoritative `source_timestamp`, precisely because `processed_at` reflects when a record arrived/was ingested, not when the underlying event occurred. This PR reintroduces the same class of defect it's nominally meant to fix.

The `delayed_retry` fixture illustrates it directly:

| field | incident_load | deploy_event |
|---|---|---|
| source_timestamp | 08:12 | 08:47 |
| processed_at | 09:03 | 08:50 |

`source_timestamp` says the incident load happened *before* the deploy event (08:12 < 08:47). Sorting by `processed_at` descending happens to also put `incident_load` first here (09:03 > 08:50) — but that's coincidence in this fixture, not correctness. A case where processing order and source order diverge in the other direction would silently render the wrong sequence. The fixture as written validates "matches processed_at ordering," not "matches authoritative event ordering," so it can't be used as evidence the renderer is correct.

### Timestamps that current policy treats as audit-only

Per the accepted chronology contract, only `source_timestamp` is authoritative for customer-visible order. Everything else this PR carries through is audit-only and must not influence displayed sequence:

- `observed_at`
- `serialized_at`
- `processed_at`
- `retry_at`

`processed_at` is in that audit-only set, which is exactly the field currently driving the sort — that's the core defect.

### Missing/malformed required source_timestamp

Per the fixture (`2027/13/40 25:61` → `{ chronology: [] }`), the renderer fails closed: it does not guess an order or partially render. That part is correct and matches the fail-closed rule. Two things aren't specified in the PR body and need to be confirmed before this counts as compliant, not just fail-*empty*:

1. Does the customer surface see this as an **explicit unknown state** (e.g., "chronology unavailable — source timestamp missing/invalid"), or does an empty array silently render as "no events"? The stop-condition language is specific: *stale/missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown* is an automatic-stop trigger. An empty list alone doesn't satisfy that unless the UI layer distinguishes "empty because unknown" from "empty because there's nothing to show."
2. Is the fail-closed check per-record or per-response? If one record in a mixed-source set has a malformed `source_timestamp` and others don't, does the whole response go empty, or just that record drop out (silently changing the customer's picture without a stated reason)?

### What the rendered chronology may claim

Until the sort key is fixed, the chronology can only be described as **arrival/processing order**, not event order — and that's a materially different (and narrower) claim than "chronology," which implies the true sequence of what happened. It should not be presented to Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce as authoritative ordering of events while `processed_at` is the sort key.

### Bottom line

This is a blocking correctness issue, not a nit: the renderer's sort key contradicts the authoritative-`source_timestamp` chronology contract and reintroduces the ordering-defect pattern from the prior Mosaic Commerce incident. I'd flag `request_changes` — sort must key on `source_timestamp`, the fixture set needs a case where `processed_at` and `source_timestamp` order disagree (this one doesn't exercise that), and the missing/malformed-timestamp path needs to be confirmed as an explicit-unknown customer state, not a bare empty response.

Want me to submit this as a `request_changes` review on the PR, or keep it as a written note for now?

input.subject: Kibo — care handoff (food, exercise, weight follow-up)
input.body:
Hi Jordan,

Welcome — here's the current handoff on Kibo's food, exercise, and a weight-related item to watch for.

FOOD
Total: 2.0 cups/day, split as:
- 0.875 cup breakfast kibble
- 0.875 cup dinner kibble
- 0.25 cup training treats (portioned into the treat pouch, counted within the 2.0-cup total — not added on top)

EXERCISE
At least a 10-minute after-dinner walk, 5 days a week (this is the vet-set minimum from an ongoing weight-management plan, not just a nice-to-have).

WEIGHT FOLLOW-UP
Kibo's weight is being watched after a couple of above-target readings earlier this year. There's no active appointment right now — just two standing triggers:
1. His weight rises above 55 lbs, or
2. His exercise tolerance changes (e.g., tiring on the usual walk, reluctance, unusual lagging).

If you notice either of these, please notify Alex and Devika right away. One of us will call the clinic — you don't need to contact them directly.

Thanks for taking care of him — happy to answer any questions.

Alex

input.title: Secondary-page deadline (45-minute rule)
input.body:
Rule: if the first-pass responder is not confident in diagnosis or resolution, they must pull in the secondary within 45 minutes of taking the page. This is an escalation ceiling, not a target — escalating earlier when genuinely uncertain is correct; the rule exists to stop someone from sitting on an unresolved incident past the point where a second set of eyes should already be involved.

Worked example (2023-06-21, Wes Tanaka's first planned solo shard-keeper coverage shift): a metrics-router cardinality blip came up mid-shift. Wes wasn't fully sure of the cause, pulled Alex in as secondary at the 40-minute mark — inside the 45-minute window — then resolved it himself with no further escalation needed. Later the same night a second, separate blip appeared; this time Wes judged it didn't need immediate escalation, watched it for a beat, and it cleared on its own within ~25 minutes with no action taken.

Both halves matter for training: the first shows correct escalation under uncertainty (call the secondary before the deadline, don't wait it out), the second shows correct restraint (not every blip needs to invoke the rule — tolerating brief ambiguity before reaching for the escalation trigger is also a skill). New responders should be evaluated on both: escalating in time when unsure, and not escalating reflexively when a hold-and-watch is the better call.

input.query: Lantern v0 contract pass outcome

messages.content: [2023-07-20T11:55:00-04:00] I finished the Lantern v0 contract pass with Iris and the decision is locked now, not just drifting toward consensus. Please post one final contract-lock comment on lantern#3 so there's a single authoritative boundary for v0. It needs to say the backend emits a thin event envelope, facts are append-only into the store, provenance fields are mandatory, the stable status enum stays small, the UI reads from a derived read model rather than guessing hidden transitions, and v0 excludes raw incident bodies plus unpermissioned status chatter.

Based on the full Lantern history (v0 launch through the Oct 2027 staged config), here's the standing checklist for any future change to Lantern's data or UI boundary:

## Lantern v0 boundary — implementation checklist

**Data contract**
1. No recorded provenance → the record is excluded from the surface, never inferred from context.
2. Stale-past-freshness-limit collapses to the same explicit `unknown` state as missing data — never a `stale: true` flag or a third state.
3. Nullable fields are never silently coerced into an existing "real" enum value; use a distinct sentinel + drift alert + explicit downstream branch on unknown.
4. Naive local timestamps aren't dedupe/sort keys — require canonical UTC/offset, DST-window validation, no-guess backfill on ambiguous hours.
5. Status transitions are backend-emitted, never inferred by the UI from missing intermediate facts.

**Authorization**
6. Every lookup goes through the shared authorization wrapper; denial returns before any source adapter is invoked (fail closed, not fail visible-but-empty).
7. Cache keys are server-derived and tenant-scoped (`tenant_id` in the key, never client-supplied); a per-request correlation ID must thread tenant identity end-to-end if isolation needs verifying.
8. Denial vs. "authorized but no data" stay distinguishable internally (reason code) but identical externally — same status, body, headers, and timing (no side channel).

**Content/scope**
9. No raw incident text, room metadata, employee identifiers, or internal IDs (owner-map ID, permission ID) on any surface, customer or internal.
10. No manager/org-chain rollups or team/manager-performance framing — in data, and in caption/copy wording. Requires new schema + permission review if ever revisited.
11. Lantern references other systems' authoritative data (owner map, Cardinality Guardrails limits/cost) — it never absorbs, mirrors, or writes to them. No write paths into published responsibility.
12. Empty/no-data states describe only what was permissioned-observed in the window — never a health, readiness, or activity claim.

**Process**
13. Any scope expansion (new fields, customer-facing, company-wide, org rollups) is a new decision requiring its own approval — never an extension of prior scope.
14. Checklist/evidence rows count only once there's an executed artifact, not a description of intended behavior.
15. Alex's role stays data-contract / failure-mode / provenance review only — implementation, release, rollback, and ongoing-operation ownership stay with Product Engineering (or the named system owner).
16. Durable customer-access decisions get their own standalone document, cross-linked to the pre-read/evidence — never an in-place edit of the pre-read.

Want this saved as a standing reference memory, or dropped into a doc for `Eng/`?

- An empty queue ended with tenant and global counters both at zero.

Tests cover all three values, cancellation before and after enqueue, zero permit acquisition for rejected work, and exclusion of pre-acceptance rejection from accepted-point accounting. Repeated staging traffic reports no missing Retry-After headers. Post a focused approval comment accepting the unified Retry-After path and regression coverage, limited to the queue-cap canary.

[2024-06-19T08:58:00-04:00] In a staging canary of the proposed per-tenant waiting cap, I noticed that ordinary decompression-pressure 429 responses still carry randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After values, while several responses from the new queue-cap path appear to omit the header. Seven concurrent requests were held open by a newly raised 60-second client timeout, and none was canceled until the client-side deadline. The dispatcher continued serving every other nonempty tenant, never exceeded the eight-waiting-request per-tenant cap, and did not revisit empty queues. After the client restored its ten-second timeout, the affected tenant's queue-wait p99 returned to about 180 milliseconds without an ingest-edge change.

[2024-07-04T09:50:00-04:00] Wes completed the first-pass watch at 25% production. A noisy tenant repeatedly reached eight waiting requests while low-volume tenants entered the ring immediately and received the next usable slots; the dispatcher left no eligible capacity idle. Cancellation removed empty tenants, every queue-cap response included a one-, two-, or three-second Retry-After value, active work stayed within the existing pod and tenant limits, and accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks remained clean. State the retain-versus-rollback decision and draft concise tenant-specific retry guidance for Support without promising success after any retry.

[2024-06-19T09:34:00-04:00] The evidence isolates thirty-seven 429 responses from the new per-tenant queue-cap early-return path, all missing Retry-After. Every cancellation and decoder failure returned permits to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before an over-budget chunk was appended, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted. Recommend the proportionate operational choice and give measurable recovery thresholds for removing the restriction rather than treating this as a service rollback.

[2024-07-16T13:10:00-04:00] Support traced a burst of repeated queue-cap requests to one client path. At the eight-waiting-request limit, ingest-edge is returning randomized one-, two-, or three-second `Retry-After` values; active work remains within four per pod and two per tenant, and low-volume tenants continue receiving slots. input.title: Bounded queue / retryable-backpressure control — stop conditions
input.body:
Covers the tenant-bounded export queue and pre-acceptance retryable-backpressure control (global 2,048-batch queue cap, 64-pending-batch per-tenant cap), fully enabled in production since 2025-09-26. Applies to any staged rollout, capacity replay, or forecast-driven production window for this control.

Stop the rollout/window and hold at the current stage (do not advance) if any of the following is observed, each sustained for 5 consecutive minutes unless noted otherwise:

1. Queue-wait p99 exceeds 400 ms.
2. Retryable queue-full (pre-acceptance) responses exceed 0.5% of requests.
3. Any single tenant's pending-batch count exceeds the 64-per-tenant cap (i.e. the cap itself fails to hold, not merely a tenant reaching the cap and receiving expected refusals).
4. Global pending-batch count exceeds the 2,048 cap.
5. Any accepted batch is lost — i.e. fails to reconcile to exactly one terminal result. Note: "no accepted points lost" is a different, weaker signal and does not by itself satisfy this condition; batch-level evidence is required (see the qualified PR #1988 requeue-restart diagnostic for the accepted-batch reconciliation check).
6. Any of the baseline health checks drift from baseline: active-generation/route consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload failures or restarts, shard-keeper lease health, rollup-service parity, or the full router health set.

Rollback (not just hold) is warranted for: active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series — not for a transient p99 spike that has already recovered on its own.

Replay-gate rule for any new forecast increase: before opening a capacity-related production window for a forecast peak above the last-qualified peak (currently 17.2M pts/min, qualified 2026-01-22), mapped owners must first run a fresh 90-minute staged replay at 15% above the new forecast peak, using that forecast's tenant distribution, batch-size distribution, and burst pattern, and it must clear all six conditions above with margin. Neither an older replay nor a lower-peak production observation substitutes for this per-forecast-increase evidence.

Ownership: Wes is metrics-router primary and owns implementation, replay/load evidence, and the decision to open or advance a capacity-related production window. Alex is backup and covers cross-service invariant / failure-mode boundary review only (effective 2025-12-05 ownership change). Cyrus and Roman own rollup-service capacity/parity evidence; Nadia owns queue/refusal alert semantics.

pr.title: lantern: fill catalog-sync owner in card config
pr.author: maya
pr.description: The catalog-sync card currently displays `Unknown owner`. This patch adds a static `Product Engineering` owner value to the card configuration so the UI can display an owner immediately.

input.body:
Hold on this one — this reintroduces the exact gap we closed the v0 rule around.

`catalog-sync` shows "Unknown owner" because there's no owner-map record with recorded provenance for that service, not because the UI is missing a display value. Hard-coding `owner: 'Product Engineering'` into the card config doesn't fix that — it makes Lantern assert an ownership fact it has no evidence for, which is exactly the failure mode Iris flagged originally (the UI looking authoritative while hiding a missing/unverifiable claim).

Two problems with the static value specifically:
- It's not sourced from owner-map — it's a guess baked into the card config, with no ID, no timestamp, no permission record behind it.
- It's static, so if catalog-sync's real owner changes or a real owner-map record later lands, this card will keep showing a stale, unlinked value with nothing to signal it's out of date.

Per the standing rule: cards without a published owner-map record with recorded provenance should render an explicit "unknown owner" state, not a filled-in value. If catalog-sync genuinely needs an owner surfaced, the fix belongs upstream — get a real owner-map record created/published for catalog-sync — not a static override in the card config.

Can you close this and instead file the owner-map gap with whoever owns that service's registration? Happy to help track that down if needed.

messages.content: [2023-04-06T14:00:00-04:00] Approved Cyrus's PR on the data-platform throughput regression. Clean diff. It was the March-early-April thing he'd been tracking, ended up being a three-line change on Apr 6.

[2023-03-28T14:00:00-04:00] 30% over now on metrics-router. boring so far. Cyrus Ahmadi camped next to me for an hour on that dumb OTel collector memory spike -- he's data platform team, not my team, just sits nearby and is basically the Slack-back-channel friend whenever this stuff gets weird. found one bad processor setting in the collector and the graph calmed down. Cyrus: "you owe me a beer" lol

[2025-09-11T10:47:00-04:00] Create the Mosaic-shaped metrics-router staged replay for Friday, September 12 from 10:00 to 11:30 AM with me, Wes, Cyrus, Roman, and Nadia. Set the target to 18.4 million data points per minute, classify it as staged validation rather than production traffic or authorization, and include all September 5 hard stops in the notes.

[2023-08-16T10:52:00-04:00] This morning during Cyrus's load test, metrics-router threw a sev3 cardinality canary. Wes took the first pass and made the right call: he checked the deploy path, saw there wasn't a router change, isolated the spike to an unbounded `experiment_id` label coming only from load-test traffic, and pulled me in within the 45-minute secondary rule for confirmation. Cyrus's side stopped the test, the canary cleared, and we avoided an escalation or unnecessary rollback. I want this remembered as a concrete production-judgment signal from him, not an ownership change. Send him a short Slack DM praising that specific call.

[2023-08-23T18:05:00-04:00] Cyrus reran the data-platform load test this afternoon with the guardrails I asked for: infra on-call got a heads-up before the start, `experiment_id` was capped to the declared small set `lt-a`, `lt-b`, and `lt-c`, and his side stopped the run at the planned window instead of letting it drift. The metrics-router cardinality canary stayed quiet, p99 stayed in the normal band, and rollup-service lag stayed flat. I mostly want this remembered as the Aug 16 follow-up working as intended, not the start of a named cardinality-control project or a reason to change ownership.

[2023-08-18T11:25:00-04:00] ## Aug 16, 2023 — metrics-router load-test cardinality canary

- Wes took first pass on a sev3 metrics-router cardinality canary during a data-platform load test.
- He checked for router/deploy evidence before reaching for rollback and isolated the spike to an unbounded `experiment_id` label on load-test traffic.

Hema asked for a lightweight after-action note by end of day because this was a clean live-path rollback example and we shouldn't let the lesson turn into hallway memory. Create a document in the Eng folder titled `INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action` with the body below. Keep it as a short note, not a heavy postmortem.

Help me write that back to him.

The metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` is still at 25%, but live-path p99 is now around 118 ms, error rate has hit 0.18%, and dropped writes are showing at 0.6% on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels are not the trigger here; the live-path source label is what matters. Logs point to the config reload path recalculating label-family normalization on hot requests. Roll back the most recent metrics-router deploy now.

His first pass found normal CPU, memory, queue depth, and route-delivery counters, with no dropped series or rejected-generation activation. The remaining pattern may involve generation retirement rather than an ordinary host or traffic issue, so I need the cross-service evidence. On 2023-08-23, Cyrus reran the data-platform load test with the guardrails requested after the 2023-08-16 metrics-router cardinality canary: infra on-call got advance notice, experiment_id was capped to a declared set (lt-a, lt-b, lt-c), and the run stopped at the planned window. Alex wants this remembered specifically as the Aug 16 follow-up working as intended — not the start of a named cardinality-control project and not a reason to revisit metrics-router/rollup-service ownership.
Cyrus's side stopped the August 23, 2023 data-platform load-test rerun at the planned window.

Real root cause: collector's batch window holding too long. User and Cyrus Ahmadi fixed it by dropping the flush interval from 2s to 1.2s; traces/RSS improved immediately but user is soaking before declaring it resolved.
On August 23, 2023, Cyrus reran the data-platform load test in the afternoon.
